sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Narmada Nilotpala writes poetry in Odia. Her collection Nija Nijara Premakhetra was published by Paschima Publications in 2019.
Her contributions to Kabita Live include ନୂଆ ପୃଥିବୀ and ଦୋକାନ. The poems gathered below offer a way into her writing, with each piece connected to the edition in which it appeared.

337.intro: A Hindi poet, writing under the name Meera, with an ongoing presence in the journal.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Sabita Singh Meera writes in Hindi. Her contributor biography records her home in Jamshedpur and notes that her poetry has appeared in collections and in translation.

Her Kabita Live contributions include क्षणिका, दोहे मन क़ो मोहे and मन! आकाशगंगा. The literary platform Jay Vijay also carries her work under the name सविता सिंह ‘मीरा’, including मन आकाशगंगा and आवरण.

257.intro: Poet, critic and translator, moving between Kashmiri, Urdu and English.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Majrooh Rashid, also known as A. R. Malik, is a poet, critic and translator. He writes in Kashmiri, Urdu and English. His work brings creative writing into conversation with the study and translation of literature.

He joined the University of Kashmir’s Department of Kashmiri in 1991. His university profile records teaching in literary criticism, modern poetry, Lal Ded and Shaikh-ul-Alam. Kabita Live’s contributor biography records his later retirement as a professor.

sections.heading: Between languages.
paragraphs: His publications include Readings and Asri Kashir Shari, alongside monographs on Asad Mir and Lasa Khan Fida. His English translations have appeared in Sahitya Akademi publications, including Medieval Indian Literature.
Kabita Live brings together several of his English poems, including Drink, Return of the Bumblebee, A Complaint and Marvel. Each can be read here in its complete form.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Manorama Choudhury is a poet, songwriter and mixed-media artist originally from Berhampur, Odisha. She writes in Odia, Hindi and English, and has presented her poetry through South Asian Poets of New England and other literary gatherings.

Her Odia book Ashtanayika: Tatwa O Kabita explores the eight heroines of classical Indian aesthetics. With Jayakrushna Choudhury, she co-authored Astanayika: The Romantic Heroines from Natyasastra to Modernity, published in 2025. The book brings classical scholarship and poetry into a discussion of love, longing and their expression in the arts.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Debarati Sen is a poet from Kolkata whose collections include Blurred Musings and Saudade. She studied English at Presidency College, Kolkata; the author note accompanying Blurred Musings also records her work in the English Department of Presidency University.

She describes writing as a source of personal release and draws on experiences from everyday life. Blurred Musings appeared in 2022, and Saudade was published by Penprints. Her poems have also appeared in literary journals, including The Chakkar.

sources.label: Blurred Musings · author note and book listing
The Chakkar · two poems by Debarati Sen

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Paramita Mukherjee Mullick is a poet, editor and literary curator with a background in science and education. Her literary work includes promoting multilingual poetry and bringing readers and writers together through poetry events.

Her English collection Cloud Nine arranges its poems in sections named after cloud formations. Published by Inking Innovations, it gathers writing about places, people and feelings. Her poetry also appears in Piker Press, whose author archive includes My Shadow and Light Cannot Be Stopped.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Tejaswini Patil is a poet, teacher and editor who writes in Marathi, Hindi and English. She founded INNSÆI Journal and MatruAkshar, publications concerned with creative writing, translation and literary exchange.

Her poetry collections include Talons and Nets, Verses of Silence, A Glass of Time and the Hindi collection Kaainat. Talons and Nets also appeared in a bilingual English–Romanian edition from Eikon in 2017, translated by Ligia Tomoiagă.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Prabhanjan K. Mishra writes poetry in Odia and English and works as a translator, critic and editor. He is a former president of Poetry Circle, Mumbai, and formerly edited its journal Poiesis.

His poetry collections include Vigil, Lips of a Canyon and Litmus. He edited A Holi of Poetry, published by Black Eagle Books in 2023, bringing the work of seven Odia poets to English-language readers through translation. His editorial work also includes From the Master’s Loom, a collection of Fakirmohan Senapati’s stories in English.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Rashmi Mohapatra writes poetry in Odia and English. Her background includes a master’s degree in economics from Jawaharlal Nehru University and a career in banking, from which she took voluntary retirement.

The 2021 ISWAL literary handbook names three of her Odia collections: Aparahnar Geeta, Abarna Pruthibi and Aparichita Pratibimba. It also publishes her English poem The Born Dead. Her contributions to Kabita Live span both languages.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Varsha Saran writes poetry in Hindi and English. Her 2017 contributor note records her connection with Meerut and postgraduate study at Chaudhary Charan Singh University.

Her English poems have appeared in Our Poetry Archive, including O’Love, Peaceful Thoughts and On the Ashes of Time. Alongside writing for journals and anthologies, she has shared recitations through her Varsha Saran ekSrijan channel.

sources.label: Our Poetry Archive · Varsha Saran, May2017
Our Poetry Archive · January2018 contributor note

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Sujit Kumar Satapathy writes poetry in Odia and Koshli–Sambalpuri. His publications include Ichchhavati, published by Sahitya Akademi in 2015, and Nuraa, a Koshli–Sambalpuri poetry collection listed in the Akademi’s 2022–23 annual report.
He took part in Sahitya Akademi’s Yubasahiti poetry-reading programme in Bhubaneswar in April 2017. The journal’s contributor account also records his background in science teaching in Odisha.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Alok Kumar Ray is a bilingual poet from Odisha who writes in Odia and English. His teaching background is in political science, alongside a literary practice that includes poetry and anthology editing.

His English collection Sillage was published by Sankalp Publication. His Odia poetry includes Meghapanata, and he has edited the bilingual anthology Trouvaille. His poetry has also appeared in World Inkers.

sources.label: Sankalp Publication · Sillage, Google Books listing
VerbalArt · Alok Kumar Ray contributor note

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anamika Nath is a poet and writer with a professional background in forensic medicine. Her literary work appears alongside her medical and research practice; her contributor biography in The Hemlock Journal identifies her as a forensic medicine specialist.
My Wardrobe Has Mitochondrial DNA was longlisted for the Wingword Poetry Prize in 2023. In 2026, The Certificates was shortlisted in The Hemlock Journal’s Still I Rise poetry contest.

sources.label: Wingword Poetry Prize · My Wardrobe Has Mitochondrial DNA
The Hemlock Journal · Still I Rise shortlist,16August2026

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Prahallad Satapathy is a bilingual poet from Balangir who writes in Odia and English. A retired associate professor of economics, he has contributed poetry to literary magazines and anthologies.

Srujan published his poem Staircase of Bones in its inaugural 2021 issue. His work also appears in Sahitya Akademi’s Indian Literature: Life Spent with Shadows was published in the January–February 2020 issue.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Antara Mukherjee is a poet, short-story writer and English-literature teacher whose work also encompasses cultural-heritage research. Her academic activity includes research on Abanindranath Tagore’s garden house at Konnagar and women’s cotton craft in West Bengal.

Her poem Expression appears in The Wise Owl. Alongside creative writing, she has presented research on Bengal’s shared cultural histories, including food, craft and the relationship between place and memory.

sources.label: Durgapur Government College · English research record
The Wise Owl · Expression and author biography

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Pravakar Satapathy (ପ୍ରଭାକର ଶତପଥୀ) is an Odia poet and editor associated with Jajpur. His Kabita Live contributor note records his earlier editorship of the literary magazine Anisha. His poetry appeared in Viswamukti’s October–November 1996 and October–December 1999 issues, placing his journal contributions within a literary practice spanning several decades.

His books include the Odia poetry collections Singhasan, available in a 2011 ebook edition, and Sabuthi Kabita, published by PEN IN Books. Sahityare Biplaba O Little Magazine, published by Athena Books, is recorded as a 2014 first edition in the Odisha government’s library-selection list.

sections.heading: Poetry and the reading community.
paragraphs: Alongside writing and editing, he has taken part in public literary gatherings. On 15 November 2013, he spoke in a discussion on promoting reading in rural communities at a National Book Trust programme in Bitana, Jajpur. Kadambini’s festival brochure also records his poetry reading at its 2014 literary festival.

sections.heading: In these poems.
paragraphs: His Kabita Live poem ମୋ କବିତା approaches poetry through images of a flower and an opening temple doorway, inviting the reader towards recognition rather than explanation. In ଟାଣ କଥା ପଦକ, a harmonium, a harsh word and the lingering mark of hurt bring the difficulty of tenderness into focus.

sources.label: National Book Trust · January 2014 newsletter, p.4

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Vikramaditya Singh writes in Hindi. His contributor biography records poetry collections and the publication of poems, short stories and essays in literary journals.

His poems in Kabita Live range from the cultural landscape of Odisha to the intimate struggle to speak against suffering. मैं ओड़िशा हूं brings temples, rivers, weaving and food into a portrait of the state. इरादे बुलंद कर लेती तो अच्छा था addresses a woman burdened by silence and urges her towards a more assertive voice.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Manju Chouhan is a poet, literary critic and English-literature academic whose contributor notes identify her with Chandigarh University. Her writing spans poetry, research and the close reading of other writers’ work.

Her poem Moon and Me appears in Poetic Anthology WPC-5, where the changing moon becomes a companion and a mirror for the speaker. Literary Voice published her review of Rupa Rao’s A Poetic Odyssey: Life and Legacy of Dr. Jernail S. Anand in its 2026 volume, adding literary biography to the subjects of her critical writing.

sources.label: Poetic Anthology WPC-5 · Moon and Me, p.77
Literary Voice · A Poetic Odyssey review

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Annwesa Abhipsa Pani writes poetry alongside work in organisation and people development. Her contributor account in Borderless connects her literary practice with the study of English literature and records her association with Pune.

Borderless published her poem Alive in December 2025. In Kabita Live, The Last Cartographer imagines memory as a way of mapping the lives of loved ones, while The Girl Who Walks in My Ink asks what writing can do in the face of a young girl’s death. Both poems give silence and absence a vivid physical presence.

sources.label: Borderless · Alive and contributor note, December 2025

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Arun Sahu, also published as Arun Kumar Sahu, is a diplomat and bilingual writer in Odia and English. His work includes essays, fiction and poetry. His English publications include Iguana and Other Poems (2020) and Trinidad and Tobago: A Diplomat’s Cultural Expedition (2022).

Light Green Eyes appeared in an English–Bulgarian edition from Academia Znanie in 2025, with Bulgarian translations by Zdravka Evtimova. His Kabita Live poem The Spring turns an ordinary act of hospitality—a fire and a cup of tea for a stranger—into an unexpected change of season.

sources.label: Embassy of India, Sofia · Arun Kumar Sahu biography
National Library of Bulgaria · 2026 bibliography, entry82

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Aishwariya Laxmi is an author, poet, editor and book blogger based in Chennai. Her debut collection, Birds of Paradise: Poems on Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness, was published by Alien Buddha Press in 2024. Her website, Aishwariya’s LittLog, brings together her poetry, book reviews and reflections on writing.

In her Kabita Live poem I’m a writer, the work of writing includes the thinking that remains invisible to others. Its conversational lines turn questions of showing and telling into a gentler reminder: a writer’s worth cannot be measured by how much of that effort is seen.

books.title: Birds of Paradise: Poems on Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Abeera Mirza is a poet from Gujrat, Pakistan, whose work has appeared in Raven Cage Zine and Orfeu. In a 2023 interview with The Mount Kenya Times, she described finding inspiration in everyday experience, nature and small moments that can pass unnoticed. She also spoke about the challenge of finding words for complex feelings.

Her Kabita Live poem The Waterfall gives a personal ambition the persistence of flowing water. Rocky paths, repeated falls and the effort of climbing carry its movement towards achievement; the speaker’s determination holds the poem together.

sources.label: Raven Cage Zine94 · contributor biography, p.94
The Mount Kenya Times · interview,2 October2023, p.24

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Aiswarya Pradhan writes poetry in Odia and is associated with Bhawanipatna in Kalahandi. Her collection ତୁମେ ଗଲାପରେ is named in her contributor note in Satyabadi’s August 2026 issue and in a regional report on the Devagiri literary honours.

Her Kabita Live poems find large emotional questions in ordinary things. ସାବୁନ୍ turns a bar of soap into a meditation on possession, touch and the wish to wash away the past. ପସରା ବିକୁଥିବା ଝିଅ follows a young seller whose load carries the weight of hunger, hope and a future still to be secured.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Amanita Sen is a Kolkata-based poet, translator and literary critic. Her collections include Candle in My Dream, published by Writers Workshop, and What I Don’t Tell You, published by Authorspress. Her work with The Antonym includes poetry editing, interviews and translations from Bengali.

With Amitava Sen, she edited Chime of Time: Yearbook of Bengali Poetry in Translation, published by The Antonym Collections in 2025. Her Kabita Live poem To my son moves from a mother’s tear to memories of infancy, then towards autumn and the passing years. Its final gesture finds in the child a poem beyond writing.

books.title: Chime of Time: Yearbook of Bengali Poetry in Translation
books.detail: Co-edited with Amitava Sen · The Antonym Collections,2025

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anita Panda is a Mumbai-based poet writing in English and Hindi. Her collection Songs of My Soul appeared in 2023. She also brought together Genesis (2021), a volume of poems by her late brother, Colonel Surya Panda, preserving his writing as a literary tribute.

Her poem Broken but undaunted appeared in Setu in June 2025. In Kabita Live’s तू कशि़श और नज़्म है, an insistent address urges its listener to break restrictions and claim the freedom to write her own story. Images of flight, rivers and an open sky give that encouragement a physical energy.

sources.label: Setu · Special Edition: Anita Panda, June2025
Odisha News Times · Songs of My Soul launch, February2023

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anjali Pattnaik writes poetry in Odia. Her contributor note records publication in literary journals and magazines, and her Kabita Live poems move between intimate reflection and social satire.

In ମୁଁ ଯେବେ ନଈ ହେଇଯାଏ, the speaker becomes a river and then a drifting leaf, finding in their movement the vulnerability of love. ମୁଁ ଗୋଟେ ସାଧାରଣ ଲୋକ takes a sharply different voice: its self-described ordinary man exposes his own cruelty, dependence and indifference. The poem lets his repeated claim to ordinariness become an indictment.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Afruja Akhtar is an Assamese poet, writer, translator and teacher associated with Duliajan. The MockingOwl Roost’s contributor note records her study of English and Assamese literature and places her within the journal’s international creative community.

Her Kabita Live poem Love in quest gathers clouds, dark wings and entwined hands into a brief encounter shaped by desire. Its movement towards memory and sweet deception unsettles the intimacy of its opening. The concentrated imagery carries the emotional turn without a long narrative explanation.

sources.label: The MockingOwl Roost · Volume2 Issue3 contributor note

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Aakash Nayak’s poem Skeleton appears in Kabita Live’s July 2024 edition. A serpent’s skeleton and an anthill form its small, shifting world: grains, insects and the spaces inside the remains become the poem’s points of attention.

As stars seem to emerge from an ant’s mouth, the scale opens from the minute to the vast. The closing insistence on luminosity brings light into a scene built from darkness and remains. The poem offers a distinctive introduction to the writer through image and transformation.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Abanindra Udgata writes in Odia and English after a career with the Reserve Bank of India. His contributor note places him in Bhubaneswar; a 2016 Impact Investors Council document records his role as Principal Chief General Manager in the bank’s Financial Inclusion and Development Department.

In Kabita Live, ଭୋକର ଅନ୍ୟନାମ lets hunger change shape, from familiar daily life to war, love and the writing of poetry. ସେଇ ଲୋକ ଜଣକ, a tribute to Ramakanta Rath, remembers the poet through trees, hills and recurring acts of recognition. Landscape becomes a way for a voice to remain present.

sources.label: Impact Investors Council ·6 January2016 letter, p.1

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anish Kanjilal is a Kolkata-based poet and educator. His collections include Fateless 13, published by Partridge, and 11 Oracles, published by White Falcon Publishing. His work draws on myth and spiritual imagery to examine human choices, loss and survival.

Kabita Live’s The Last Faith brings the wooden form of Jagannath into conversation with ecological destruction and figures from several religious and mythic traditions. The Man in White returns to a repeated chorus as light, winter and bodily endurance change around its central figure. Both poems give abstract questions a strongly visual setting.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ashish Vidyarthi contributes Hindi poetry to Kabita Live. His poem जिंदगी जिंदादिली का नाम है appears in the April 2024 edition and centres on a small, everyday gesture: a smile offered in the midst of difficulty.

The poem imagines happiness flowering from the mud of sorrow. Short stanzas move from the inward life to encounters with others, returning at the close to the opening encouragement to smile. Its direct address gives the verse the warmth of spoken reassurance.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anju Kapoor is a Bahrain-based poet and visual artist who writes in English and Hindi. The Cultural Reverence published her illustrated poem HER in June 2024, crediting both the verse and the painting to her. Her writing brings the inward life into conversation with images drawn from the natural world.

In Kabita Live’s A Circle - Its Bearing on my Life, the circle expands from the beginnings of life to time, feeling and uncertainty. A butterfly, roots and fruit, and pearls gathered into a necklace carry the poem through successive transformations. The recurring definition of the circle gives these changing images a shared centre.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ashok Bhargava is a Vancouver-based poet and photographer who writes in English and Hindi. His collections include Skipping Stones, Mirror of Dreams, A Kernel of Truth and Lost in the Morning Calm. His author website brings his poetry and photography together with records of literary community activity.

Kabita Live’s Maya - Illusion uses very short stanzas to unsettle the certainty of knowing. The speaker moves from I and you to we and they, repeatedly handing knowledge from one side to the other. Its final turn towards illusion makes the spare pattern into a meditation on perception.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Alka Nigam is a Lucknow-based Hindi writer associated with Lafzon Ki Potli. Her signed poetry on YourQuote carries both that name and the city, while the first issue of Brahmand: Voice of the Cosmos also identifies her as a contributor. Her work includes poetry and prose.

In Kabita Live’s छिन्नमस्तिका, an insistent address draws on Sita, Panchali, Gargi and goddess imagery. The poem moves from flowers and adornment to resolve and confrontation, ending with the fierce form named in its title. Its repeated commands and closing refrain give the piece an emphatic spoken rhythm.

sources.label: Brahmand: Voice of the Cosmos · Volume1 Issue1

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Avantika Vijay Singh is a writer, editor, poet and photographer. Her poetry books include Flowing… in the river of life and Dancing Motes of Starlight. She also writes Ordinary People, Extraordinary Lives for the Times of India, bringing everyday experience into a different, often humorous register.

Her Kabita Live poem Amaltas… begins with the yellow flowers of summer and opens into a remembered landscape from the Ramayana. The flowering tree connects a present moment of looking with Ram’s journey towards Sugriv and the hills of Rishyamukha. Nature becomes a meeting place for observation and story.

sources.label: Times of India · Ordinary People, Extraordinary Lives

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Aparna Pradhan writes in Hindi and English and also works as an artist. Trained in zoology, she contributes poetry and articles to literary publications; her essay on Awadhi cuisine appeared in the Journal of Asian Arts, Culture and Literature. Literary Warriors Group records the launch of her books नारी अस्मिता and त्रिआयामी at its 2023 New Delhi festival.

Her Kabita Live poems bring questions of dignity and belonging into direct speech. छुअन asks the reader to recognise a woman’s inward life beyond her body. आख़िर क्यूँ – परायेपन का दंश follows a woman from her childhood home to marriage, asking why neither place grants her an unquestioned sense of belonging.

sources.label: JAACL · The Delicate Flavors of Awadhi Cuisine

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Aparna Mohanty is an Odia poet, translator and critic associated with Kendrapara. Her collection ଝିଅପାଇଁ ଝର୍କାଟିଏ received the Odisha Sahitya Akademi Award for 2007. Alongside her poetry, her literary work includes translation, criticism and a career teaching Odia; festival records recognise her sustained attention to women’s experience.

In Kabita Live’s ଦାରୁଣ ଅସହାୟତା, memories of the freedom struggle become a question addressed to the present. The poem contrasts sacrifice and the hope of human dignity with the language of ceremonial remembrance. Its repeated question about the meaning of a country gives the closing sense of helplessness its force.

sources.label: The New Indian Express · Akademi award announcement

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Aarti Mittal, also known as Rita Jain, writes poetry in English and Hindi. Her Kabita Live contributor note places her in Mumbai and describes her work with children’s skits. Her poem A Woman appeared in Our Poetry Corner, where the byline Aarti Mittal and the signature Rita connect the names she uses in her writing.

Her Kabita Live contributions range from the flowing-water metaphor of REFLECTIONS to the unsettling enclosed space of Hello. Fearless warrior uses the imagined voice of a child to confront the absence of safety among the living. Across these poems, changes in image and voice make room for both resilience and protest.

sources.label: Wonderful Women of Excellence · Aarti Mittal personal account

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anita Ray’s ନିଜକୁ ଖୋଜିବାକୁ ପଡ଼େ appears in Kabita Live’s June 2023 edition. The poem follows a speaker searching for a self among familiar people, shifting expectations and the demands of an inward life.

A leaf scorched by dry heat waits for rain, while silence carries the memory of closeness. These images give physical shape to uncertainty and longing. The poem moves towards an unresolved ache rather than an easy answer, keeping the search in its title open.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Asish Kumar Mishra writes in Odia and is associated with Subarnapur. His literary work also appears on StoryMirror under the name Ashish Kumarmishra, where a signed contribution identifies the same district. Kabita Live introduces him through the poem ଦୁଃଖ.

The flower and the bee give this poem its recurring image of trust and hurt. Petals, fragrance and wind hold the feeling in the natural world before the final stanza turns directly towards another person. Sorrow becomes a paradox: something endured, yet also something the speaker fears losing.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ananya Goswami contributes Ashes to Kabita Live’s April 2023 edition. Her contributor note describes an enduring interest in art and literature; the poem itself offers a searching encounter with grief, survival and the difficult work of beginning again.

Waves, darkness and drifting ashes give suffering a landscape. The phoenix appears as a possibility, but the poem resists the comfort of an effortless rebirth. Its closing movement asks what it takes to go on living when the self must find a path through its own ruins.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ajit Dash writes poetry in English, with interests that extend to language and public life. His contributor biography in Literary Vibes identifies the collections Midnight Dream and Wings of Burning Violin. The journal has also published his poems Sriram and Lotus.

In Kabita Live’s Mother Bharati, an invocation grows into a vision of cultural and civic renewal. Figures from the Ramayana and Mahabharata stand beside questions about language, learning and social hierarchy. The poem’s address to a mother figure gives these public concerns the cadence of an appeal.

sources.label: Literary Vibes · April2026 poems and contributor note

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Akhil Kumar Mishra writes poetry in Odia and English. His English collection Painted Silence was published by Timepass in 2018 and is catalogued by the Gandhi Smriti Library at LBSNAA. His work in public broadcasting has run alongside his literary interests; in March 2026, he presided over a Maya Sahitya gathering in Bhubaneswar devoted to literature and its place in society.

His Kabita Live poem ଅଧା ବାଟ turns towards a journey left unfinished. A green morning, an uneasy reflection and a mountain of sorrow on shifting sand bring hope and instability into the same space. The address to a companion who stopped halfway makes the distance emotional as well as physical.

sources.label: Gandhi Smriti Library, LBSNAA · Painted Silence
Press Information Bureau · Maya Sahitya gathering, March2026

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anindita Bose is a poet, editor and literary organiser associated with Kolkata. Her collections include I Know the Truth of a Broken Mirror and Illuminating Darkness. She co-edited The Kolkata Cadence with Jagari Mukherjee and Inam Hussain Mullick, bringing together contemporary voices from the city. Chair Poetry Evenings lists her as festival manager; its 2024 programme also records the launch of Youthful Elegies: Echoes of a New Generation 2024, which she edited.

Her Kabita Live poems return to the work of tending an inner life. Mrittika finds a grounding presence in soil and the living world, while Mothers’ Day on Earth measures longing through the absence of a mother’s physical presence. Path of Consciousness and Existence & Essence question how a self can stay rooted amid change; Fluttering Hearts gives that restless search a more defiant movement.

books.title: The Kolkata Cadence: Contemporary Kolkata Poets

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Angurbala Parida is an Odia poet associated with Rourkela. Sahitya Akademi records her participation in its Asmita programme for Odia women writers in Bhubaneswar on 17 July 2013, where she read Rabana and Balada. The event placed her work in a conversation about women’s experience, identity and the pressures of social life.

In Kabita Live’s ନାରୀ ପରି ମରୁଥାଏ ନଈ, the river and the woman mirror one another: both sustain life, endure restraint and face the loss of a name. ପ୍ରେମ ସରିବା ଦିନ widens the question of love into a landscape of violence and ruins. Against that devastation, the continuing flow of the Kathajodi and Mahanadi offers a counter-image.

sources.label: Odisha Culture Department · Publishers’ Directory of Odisha

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Adyasha Das writes across poetry, travel and cultural heritage. Her work with the Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management in Bhubaneswar connects teaching and research with an interest in the places and traditions of Odisha. Her books include The Yogini Poems: Love and Life and The Chausathi Yoginis of Hirapur: From Tantra to Tourism, approaching the Yoginis through both poetry and cultural study.

In Kabita Live’s Caretaker, a house becomes the shape of a life: its colours, garden and rooms hold ambition, intimacy and memory. As the speaker imagines departure, possessions give way to dates, relationships and remembered happiness. The final gift is a key, entrusted to someone asked to care for what remains.

books.title: The Yogini Poems: Love and Life

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ashok Kumar Singh, also published as Ashok Singha, writes poetry in Odia and English. His books include the Odia collection ଅପରାପର (Aparapara), published by Black Eagle Books in 2021. The bibliography accompanying that collection connects it with The Raging Tide and Quiet Shore and the bilingual ଦୃଶ୍ୟାନ୍ତର, titles also identified in his Kabita Live contributor note.

His poems here move between inward unease and the public world. Fear finds its subject in a television voice, weather and a falling petal. Invitation keeps a house lit for an absent guest, testing the boundary between welcome and withdrawal. In ଜଙ୍ଗଲ, a speaking forest turns human accusations of wildness back upon the people who conceal violence within it.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Antaryami Mishra writes in Odia and English. His Odia collection Maa Nishaada appeared in 2017, and his poetry has been featured in literary magazines including The Genius and GloMag. A GloMag contributor note from January 2021 also records his work teaching English at R.D.C. Higher Secondary School in Chilika Nuapada.

In The Road Taken, his contribution to Kabita Live, the journey gradually becomes an encounter with the poet within. Early companionship gives way to a reticent presence that is both ally and rival. Roads, veins and a following shadow connect the private act of walking with a poetic consciousness whose concerns extend beyond the self.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anjali Sahoo writes poetry in English and Odia, as well as short fiction in Odia. Her English collections include A Tryst with Thunder, Soliloquy of Eternity, An Ocean’s Autograph and Touchstone of Time. Her scholarly work also explores creativity and peace education, bringing literary practice into conversation with teaching and the imagination.

Blank Page, her Kabita Live contribution, treats unwritten space as possibility. Words pass from the end of one line into the beginning of another, creating a chain of thought and sound. The closing image of prepared land and unsown seeds turns the page into a place where a future work might take root.

sources.label: Journal of Peace Education · The creative mind and peace education

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anadi Charan Pradhan writes in Odia and English. Kabita Live’s contributor note describes a career teaching English in Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas and identifies him as a co-translator of the short-story collection Rivulets of Reflections. His poem Rain Now and Then is also named in Setu’s review of Toshali 2023: Anthology of Poetry.

The poem sets remembered childhood rain beside an increasingly unpredictable present. Fields, bullocks and children’s play give way to hail, uprooted trees and anxious waiting. Its changing portraits of the rain—from fury to an infant’s stillness—hold together the farmer’s vulnerability and the speaker’s longing for a more familiar rhythm.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Akshaya Kumar Das is a poet from Odisha and the author of The Dew Drops, an English collection published by Partridge India. His poetry has appeared in literary journals and anthologies, including The Heart of a Poet. Contributor records also document his work organising a 2017 poetry festival in Bhubaneswar under the Feelings International Artists Society.

His Kabita Live poems favour direct address and paired lines. Amazing Evolution turns from sunlight and growing trees towards a plea for coexistence. The voice of a poet imagines ink as a sustaining energy, while Life and LOVE find wonder in creativity, companionship and the small human presence within a much larger universe.

sources.label: Inner Child Press · The Heart of a Poet2020

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Agnivesh Mahapatra writes in English, Hindi and Odia and also works as a translator and editor. His book Midnight Musings gathers poems in the form he calls Trione, and he edited the anthology Moontide. The Antonym published his English translation of Suryasnata Tripathy’s Odia poem Quietness in April 2024.

His Kabita Live contributions often make discovery a conversation. Present—Trench—Future turns aspiration and routine into a landscape to cross. The Place to Seek looks for the touch or attention that opens a person, a building or a remembered place. In अग्नि की कलम, the stalled pen becomes an invitation to act and to write beyond private concerns.

sources.label: The Antonym · Quietness, translated by Agnivesh Mahapatra

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Arti Kumari writes poetry in Hindi and English and is also a ghazal writer and editor. Her collections include धड़कनों का संगीत and साथ रखना है. She has edited ये नए मिज़ाज का शहर है and बिहार की महिला ग़ज़लकार, while Rekhta carries a selection of her ghazals. Reviewing धड़कनों का संगीत in Setu, Subhash Pathak “Ziya” draws attention to the meeting of love and social protest in her work.

Her Kabita Live poem True love speaks in direct, rhyming appeals. It sets love outside the calculation of profit and loss, then moves towards devotion, vulnerability and giving. The final images of melting ice and a disappearing drop carry its idea of surrender into the natural world.

sources.label: Lahak Digital · Arti Kumari ghazals and contributor biography

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Amit Shankar Saha is a poet, short-story writer and literary scholar. His books range from Balconies of Time and Illicit Poems to Etesian::Barahmasi and Undecember: The Thirteenth Month. The latter arranges thirty poems around the waxing and waning phases of a lunar month. His author website also records his editorial work with EKL Review and his scholarship on Indian diasporic writing.

In Kabita Live, his poems turn ordinary acts into questions about language and intimacy. Waves lets reading become an ocean shared between minds. Arrival finds its poem in the very act of waiting for one, while Denture uses an artificial tooth and everyday conversation to approach the distance created by another person’s silence.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Archana Bahadur Zutshi is a poet and translator whose collections include Poetic Candour, The Speaking Muse, Careless Verse Whispers and Full Throated Stirrings. In her essay for The Culturium, she describes poetry growing from speech, childhood song-making and an early familiarity with Urdu, Hindi and English literature. Her published translation work includes five poems by Suryakant Tripathi “Nirala” in the Indian Journal of Comparative Literature and Translation Studies.

Rainbow, her Kabita Live contribution, brings scent and colour into a single experience. Incense, flowers and rain open onto an inward rainbow, then widen into a vision of celebration shared across different names and traditions. Its movement from breath to sky gives the poem an intimate beginning and an expansive close.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Anu Girdhar brings together a background in dental teaching and a poetry practice that began during the lockdown. Her contributor biography at Rhyvers describes that beginning, while her collection As the Life Unfolds follows the changing emotional experiences of a woman’s life. Her books also include Heartstrings, recorded in Kabita Live’s contributor note and a 2022 Tribune book notice.

In “Intimacy,” her contribution to Kabita Live, closeness is built through repeated acts of attention: choosing one another, listening, caring and accepting vulnerability. The poem moves from passion towards a gentler understanding of love as mutual recognition and healing.

sources.label: The Tribune · 2 October 2022 book notice (preserved scan)

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Amiya Ranjan Mohapatra’s Odia poem “ହାଃ, ଜୀବନ” appears in Kabita Live’s January 2023 edition. Its imagined museum offers a striking entrance into the poem: old tears and rustless smiles become objects to be displayed, while visitors arrive carrying longing, tenderness and unfinished desires.

The playful language of tickets and customers gradually gives way to a poet’s funeral procession. A rainbow, fading flowers and a river of fire carry the poem towards its closing image of life as sunlight and shadow—present, yet always slipping away.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Adyasha Priyadarshini contributed “Embracing Winter” to Kabita Live’s December 2022 edition. Her contributor note describes a love of reading and a writing practice that began as a way of expressing emotion.

The poem welcomes winter through small bodily sensations: cold ears, dry lips, a misted window and the comfort of a blanket. Its voice moves from playful reluctance to leave that comfort towards the warmth of friends gathered around a Christmas tree, finding companionship within the season’s chill.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Aneek Chatterjee writes poetry and fiction alongside his work in international relations. His publisher’s biography records a doctorate in that subject and a Fulbright visit to the University of Virginia. His poetry collections include Seaside Myopia, Unborn Poems and Yellow Prison, and Archive Avenue; The Funeral Procession is a novel.

His Kabita Live poems move between intimate memory and public unease. “Warmth” recalls a clay oven and an elder sister through the ache of their absence, while “Blindfolded” exposes the uneasy comfort of refusing to look at injustice. In “Waiting For The Red Soil On My Skin,” the speaker imagines an education and a society renewed through water, soil and trees; “Future” makes room for uncertainty rather than a predetermined life.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Amita Roy, whose books also appear under the name Amita Ray, is a poet, short-story writer and translator with a background in teaching English in Kolkata. Her work includes the poetry collection Until Birds Sing, the stories of Trail of Love and Longings, and translations from Bengali, among them Abanindranath Tagore’s Khirer Putul. A Setu review of Treats in Translation discusses her attention to the atmosphere and emotional texture of Bengali stories carried into English.

Her Kabita Live poems make absence tangible through ordinary surroundings. In “Parallel Thoughts,” coffee, music and the movement of a café accompany an increasingly weary wait. “Displacement” gathers fragments of sky, shade, breeze and green into the difficult work of making a home after leaving familiar roots.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Arundhati Mohanty contributes Odia poetry to Kabita Live. Her contributor note records postgraduate study at Vani Vihar and a doctorate from Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan. “ତୁମେ ଏକା ଜଣେ,” published in the magazine’s first edition, offers a searching meditation on what it means to be protected.

The poem’s high walls, locked doors and sheltered courtyard turn safety into confinement. Against that enclosure, the speaker imagines stepping out into sunlight, monsoon rain and the world beyond familiar boundaries. Its ending holds independence and trust together: a willingness to venture out, and faith that one beloved presence will still search for the speaker.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Binay Laha’s literary work includes poetry and the editing of Indology, an English little magazine associated with Raiganj in West Bengal. His Setu contributor biography names Auction of My Soul, The Wife of Red Soil and Bad Boy Good Girl among his books. He also co-edited Voices Now: World Poetry Today with Braja K. Sorkar, bringing together an international selection of poetry.

In “My love,” his Kabita Live contribution, companionship becomes a source of balance and possibility. The brief stanzas move from a shared smile to the image of a canvas on which a life can be painted, while leaving the beloved’s mystery intact.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Banasmita Pati’s writing moves between English fiction and Odia poetry and adaptation. BlueRose lists The Ivory Man and Journey to the Island of Dolls among her books and places her literary practice in Bhubaneswar. B. K. Publications’ catalogue on Google Play includes Agnipariksha, a poetic engagement with the Ramayana, and Suryaputra Karna, her Odia re-creation of Ramdhari Singh Dinkar’s Rashmirathi.

In “The Missing Butterfly,” her Kabita Live poem, a watched cocoon becomes the centre of impatient predictions and gossip. Its eventual transformation occurs away from the spectators’ notice. The butterfly’s departure turns the poem towards freedom from other people’s expectations and the possibility of choosing a different future.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bandana Sahoo writes under the pen name Shibangi Dhara. Her contributor note in Srujan: The Creativity Journal places her in Jajpur and records her work in Odia, English and Hindi. That journal published her poem “Once Again” in December 2023. Her Kabita Live contribution, “Bustle Of Life,” has also been discussed alongside “Devi” in a critical essay by Nurul Hoque for Saturno Magazine.

“Bustle Of Life” moves from restlessness towards an imagined place of tenderness and renewal. Evening air, wet sand, footprints and a thorny path give physical shape to the speaker’s search for peace. The poem’s movement between weariness and hope makes intimacy a refuge from the pressures surrounding it.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bharati Hazarika is a multilingual writer from Guwahati. Her contributor profile in Gems V records work in poetry, stories and articles; the anthology includes her poems on the natural world and human equality. Kabita Live’s contributor note also describes her writing for children and her work with lyrics and music.

Her Kabita Live poems bring public concerns into direct, insistent language. “Freedom Is Our Birthright” answers physical restraint with the freedom of thought and spirit, returning to its declaration like a refrain. “Glacier” turns from the beauty of ice and its living surroundings towards an urgent appeal to care for the earth. Together, the poems move between human dignity and responsibility towards the natural world.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Badal Mohanty writes poetry and fiction in Odia and is associated with Barsha Publication in Bhubaneswar. Reports of the publisher’s literary events identify him as its director. His books include the novel Fula Rasiya Re; a report of the 2023 Barsha festival also records the launch of his novels ମାଇଚିଆ and ମାୟାମଞ୍ଚ alongside prose recollections.

In his two-part poem “ଶୂନ୍ୟସ୍ଥାନ,” a school exercise in filling blanks opens into an inquiry about absence. Childhood friendship, loss and a love remembered across forty years give the empty space changing meanings. The poem comes to value what cannot be filled: a voice, a memory, a place another person continues to occupy.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Biswanath Kundu is a Kolkata poet whose literary work also includes criticism and translation. Alongside Sabita Chakraborty, he translated fourteen short stories by K. V. Dominic into Bengali for Nirbachito Chotogalpo. The book’s introduction, written by Ramesh Chandra Mukhopadhyaya, also discusses Kundu’s English collection Poetry Dot 6, illustrated by Dominique de Miscault. His poems “Mirage” and “Life begins at sixty” appear in Creative Flight’s April 2025 issue.

His Kabita Live contributions use rhyme and direct argument to explore shared life. “Reel life vs Real life” questions the passage from screen entertainment into everyday expectations, while “Mutual trust and understanding” traces cooperation through learning, work and family. “Needs of Gender Studies” extends this concern towards equality and the freedom to choose one’s own path.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bijay Mohapatra writes poetry and criticism in Odia. Published under the spelling Bijay Mahapatra, his collection What the River Says brings his Odia poems into English through translations by Kamala Prasad Mahapatra. Black Eagle Books describes a practice developed across four poetry collections; in his introduction to the English volume, Haraprasad Das draws attention to the allusions and layered metaphors that give this work its texture.

“ଲବଣୀ ପିତୁଳା,” his Kabita Live poem, places beauty inside a guarded enclosure and asks what it means when it cannot move freely. Fragrance, moonlight, birds and wind press against the barriers. The poem’s shifting landscape of curtains, hills and forests makes the desire for freedom both physical and elusive.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Baijnath Gupta combines poetry with the study and teaching of English literature. His journal contributions identify his association with DSN Postgraduate College, Unnao. Setu’s contributor profile records his poetry collection Echoes of a Sensitive Heart, while Creative Saplings has published both his verse and his study of ecofeminism in the poetry of Emily Dickinson and Maya Angelou.

In “Salvation,” the speaker declines release from life’s recurring cycle. A phoenix rising from ashes becomes a moth returning to a lamp, and repeated movements of coming and going carry the poem forward. Its short lines and abrupt opening questions give this meditation on desire and return an intimate, conversational voice.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bharati Nayak writes poetry in Odia and English and also works in translation. Her collections include Padma Paada in Odia and Words Are Such Perfect Traitors and A Day for Myself in English. Her collaborative work includes In the Realms of Love & Divinity with Antony Theodore, and she edited the third volume of Radical Rhythm. Quilled Ink Press also documents her Odia translation project with Adiela Akoo’s Lost in a Quatrain.

In “A Day For Myself,” the speaker asks to keep one day from a life generously given away. Flowers, butterfly colours, a cuckoo’s song, rain, sky and sea become gifts with which to renew the self and its poetry. On her author page, Nayak identifies this English poem as her translation of her own Odia poem “Nija Paain Dinatie,” making it a small meeting place between her two writing languages.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bharadwaj Mishra writes English poetry rooted in places, remembered lives and the pressures of change. His collections include Farewell to Kalpana Saikia and Bathing Ghat at Kotipalli. He is also a contributor to Chandrabhāgā, whose contributor notes connect him with the latter collection.

His poems in Kabita Live make landscape a speaking presence. In Scarecrow, an obsolete guardian of the fields confronts the arrival of a tractor; in Me, Varanasi, Beloved, the city addresses its deity through history, grief and everyday life. Mango Flowers of March sets the delicacy of seasonal blossom beside the violence and losses carried by memory.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Binati Satapathy writes in Odia; Kabita Live’s contributor record places her in Bolangir. Her poem ଶବ୍ଦଭୁକ makes the search for words a bodily and intimate act. Words sprout from dry ground, rise through breath and take the shapes of stars and flowers.
The poem moves from gathering language to offering it: words become sandalwood paste for a beloved presence. Its closing welcome sets aside pride, giving the act of writing the tenderness of a gift.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Binapani Debta’s Odia poems in Kabita Live bring the living world into conversation with human responsibility. In ନିଦ ଭିତରେ ହାତ ପ୍ରସାରେ ଶିଶୁ, a child’s outstretched hand becomes a question addressed to a generation that has consumed the earth and left too little for those who follow.

ଅଯୋଧ୍ୟା turns a familiar epic landscape toward justice, courage and the voices of the vulnerable. In ଜଣେ କବି ନୀରବ ହୋଇଗଲେ, rivers, birds and trees gather around a silent poet: poetry continues through attention and breath, even when its maker tries to withdraw.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bichitra Dash writes in Odia; Kabita Live’s contributor record places her in Puri. In ଠିକ୍ ରାତି ବାରଟା ବାଜିଲେ, midnight opens a space where longing can fly, dreams can be washed in a river of words, and love can be planted in the ground of trust.

Daybreak brings a harder world of daily necessities. The poem follows that movement from intimate possibility to exhaustion, ending with the speaker’s plea for air and the sense of a life divided into too many parts.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Binod Kumar writes Hindi poetry under the pen name Ballopuri. His Kabita Live poem हवा सर्दी की.. begins with the sensations of changing seasons: cold that makes the body tremble, summer’s restlessness, and spring awakening memories of a beloved.

Across three short stanzas, wind becomes more than weather. It shifts direction like circumstance, sustains everyone through breath, and finally turns into a figure for influence and power. The repeated opening gives the poem a conversational rhythm as it moves between nature and social observation.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bebina Rath writes in Odia and is also known as Smita in Kabita Live’s contributor record. Her poem ଆଲ୍‌ଜାଇମର୍ସ୍‌ begins with the remembered presence of a father and an empty wheelchair, using ordinary household objects to hold the weight of absence.

As the poem develops, the family’s failure to listen becomes a larger question about the country and its moral bearings. The movement between private grief and public unease gives its recurring memory of the father a force beyond the household.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bijayalaxmi Rath writes in English, Hindi and Odia. Her literary work accompanies a background in English teaching: the contributor note in Literary Vibes records her master’s degree from Utkal University and teaching at St Xavier International School in Bhubaneswar. Her poems appear in Literary Vibes, and she reported on the first Toshali Literature Festival for Setu in 2023.

The poems gathered here often connect an inward change with a season or landscape. August Melts finds renewed hope in rain and green growth; Last Decoration of Departure uses autumn to consider solitude and acceptance. Persona desires to be Louder turns toward self-worth, giving the inner life a voice of its own.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bibhu Padhi is a poet and translator from Cuttack, educated at Ravenshaw College. His poetry collections include Going to the Temple and Lines from a Legend, published by Peepal Tree Press in 1993. Alongside his own writing, he has brought Odia poetry into English, including poems by Bibek Jena published in The Caravan.

In Rivers, his contribution to Kabita Live, the changing water becomes a measure of time beyond the human scale. Its quiet couplets follow the river from a thin trickle to overwhelming force, contrasting that ancient movement with the smaller commitments of family and daily life.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Binaya Kumar Mohanty writes in Odia. The biography supplied to Kabita Live places his beginnings in Anduli, Kendrapara, and records a background in teaching animal science. His poems here bring private uncertainty into contact with the larger failures of power, ambition and public life.

In “ବଡପଣ”, a broken kite-string and Ravana’s disguise unsettle appearances of greatness; even lovers prepare for battle. “ମୁଁ ଶୋଇ ପଡୁଛି” sets grand pursuits against a suffering earth and a speaker unable to help. The more intimate “ରିଜୋଲ୍ୟୁସନ” casts love letters into the Brahmani, only to discover that the heart cannot discard its memories so easily. Across these poems, disillusionment makes room for both anger and a quieter willingness to receive whatever comes.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Boby Borah writes in English. Kabita Live’s supplied biography connects her with Shankardev Shishu Niketan in Doom Doom, Assam, as its founder and principal. In the poems gathered here, rivers, rain, flowers and birds become ways of speaking about longing, loss and the search for belonging.

“For You” gives waiting a succession of natural forms: wind, fireflies, dust and sunlight. “The Girl” moves from a wish to become a river towards the image of Durga, while “That city was not for me” returns insistently to the ache of estrangement. Her questions also reach beyond intimate feeling: “If Ever Said” challenges religious division and possession through the shared claims of humanity, conscience and the earth.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bipin Naik, also published as Bipin Nayak, is an Odia poet whose collection Swarachitra received the Odisha Sahitya Akademi Award. His work is available in English in The Painted Voice, translated by Namita Laxmi Jagaddeb. In an interview, he describes poetry as emerging from experience and the subtler movements of the mind, with words carrying more than their surface meanings.

His poem “ନିରଞ୍ଜନା” turns an address to a river into a search for release and stillness. Its two movements pass from the wish to leave the safety of the shore to the surrender of crown, ornaments and worldly identity. The forest journey, disciplined seeking and shade of the riverside peepal tree give the poem a contemplative force: longing becomes a prayer to be washed and brought to rest.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Braja K Sorkar is a Bengali–English poet, editor and translator. His literary work includes editing the Bengali journal Tristoop and the anthology Voices Now: World Poetry Today, as well as translating Assamese poet Hiren Bhattacharya into Bengali. His English collection Syllables of Broken Silence brings another language to a practice shaped by sustained reading, attention to craft and the inner life.

In his Kabita Live poems, silence is rarely empty. “A lost tune” listens for the uncertain return of intimacy, while “Crafts” imagines the self assembled from the syllables of existence. “Dark Matters After All” moves between the universe, painting and the night, searching darkness for a creative beginning. The paired poems gathered as “Two poems” carry that searching voice through time, nature and the difficult making of a shared home.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bhagyashree Mishra is a writer from Sunabeda, Odisha, with a professional background in software engineering. Alongside poetry, she writes short stories, essays and brief forms. Her contributor biographies describe an interest in nature, social concerns, love and patriotism—concerns that meet in the poem she shares with Kabita Live.

“I hug you in my dreams” gives voice to a soldier’s wife waiting through a long separation. Domestic sounds, remembered embraces and falling maple leaves lead into the distant extremes of Siachen and the Thar. The poem holds tenderness beside duty: its final awakening does not end the longing, but asks the speaker to carry it with strength.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Balaram Pujari’s Odia poems in Kabita Live bring the wounded earth and the struggle for words into close relation. Their imagery is dense and urgent: forest, mountain, breath and weaponry become part of a language confronting injury and uncertainty.

In “ନାଦନୈବେଦ୍ୟ”, an assaulted forest and a fainting earth call for care amid the violence of machinery. “ପ୍ରୟାଣ ପ୍ରହର” turns words into missiles, empty quivers and a departing vessel, asking how a life can still be written when language itself seems under siege. Read together, the poems make speech feel both endangered and necessary.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bhagirathi Mishra is an Odia poet whose collections include Akasha Khoja. Kabita Live’s supplied biography also records his work translating world poetry into Odia. His place in the wider literary conversation is reflected in Sahitya Akademi’s 2022 programme, which listed him to speak about the life and writing of Srinibas Udgata.

“ଦୃଶ୍ୟ ଦୃଶ୍ୟାନ୍ତର” builds its argument through a sequence of sharply contrasting scenes: blood at a city crossing, a child beside a begging mother, a visitor absorbed in colourful kites. Hunger and spectacle occupy the same field of vision. The poem’s satire of traded dreams and imported sleep returns to a searching question about what a maker of images chooses to conceal—and what open eyes continue to see.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bidyutaprava Gantayat, also published as Bidyut Prabha Gantayat, is an Odia poet and translator with a background in teaching chemistry. Her writing includes children’s literature and haiku, while her translations bring other Indian voices into Odia. Sahitya Akademi published her translation of Ashok Vajpeyi’s Keunthi Nahin Seithi; her literary biographies also record translations of Mahadevi Verma.

Her two Kabita Live contributions move between private hurt and public menace. “Scattered” finds the persistence of absence in an old diary, fallen petals and a solitary lamp. In “ମଦାରୀର ମନ୍ତ୍ର ଫୁଙ୍କା”, the commanding performer becomes an image of coercion: dazzling speech and fear give way to violence, leaving a troubling question about the obedience of those who remain.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Babita Mohapatra is an Odia poet with a background in law and social work in Rourkela. Rourkela College records her participation as an advocate and speaker in its programme on sexual harassment. Her poems in Kabita Live attend closely to women’s emotional lives and to the unequal demands placed upon them.

“ସ୍ତ୍ରୀଲୋକ” challenges a relationship in which one person’s freedom depends on the other’s endless giving. “ବର୍ଷା ଭିଜା ସ୍ତ୍ରୀଲୋକ” takes rain as a more complicated image: it washes tears and nourishes life, yet cannot promise shelter to the woman who sustains others. Both poems move through direct address, questioning and vivid bodily imagery, making generosity inseparable from a demand to be seen.

sources.label: Rourkela College: Anti Sexual Harassment Cell

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bipin Patsani is an English-language poet from Odisha whose teaching career took him to Arunachal Pradesh. His collections include Voice of the Valley, published by Writers Workshop in 1993, and Another Voyage and Homecoming, both published in 2010. His work has appeared in Kavya Bharati and other literary journals, joining a long engagement with poetry to questions of culture and human conduct.

In “The Taste of Freedom”, freedom depends on compassion, honesty and shared responsibility. “GROWING BIG AND BEAUTIFUL” asks whether monuments and rituals are enough to sustain a civilisation, while “PRIDE AND ANIMOSITY” challenges the destruction of the past in the name of prestige. “GOD, A POETIC IMAGE” brings these concerns into a contemplative register, imagining a divine presence spacious enough to gather different symbols and forms of experience.

books.title: Voice of the Valley
books.detail: English poetry · Writers Workshop, 1993 · Publisher catalogue

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bhagaban Jayasingh writes poetry in Odia and English and works as a critic, editor and translator. His Odia collection Pheranti Ghar received the Odisha Sahitya Akademi award. Through anthologies such as Footprints of Fire and The Birds in the Storm, he has also brought modern Odia poetry to readers in English.

His poems in Kabita Live approach death through the lives that continue around an absence. In “Grandmother”, a child’s explanations of mortality cannot ease a widow’s grief. In “ଜଣେ କବିଙ୍କ ମୃତ୍ୟୁ ପରେ”, the world carries on after a poet’s death, while remembrance itself becomes uncertain. The domestic and the cosmic meet in these questions of what remains when someone is gone.

books.title: The Birds in the Storm
books.detail: Modern Odia poetry in English translation · Notion Press, 2024 · Book preview

sources.label: The Birds in the Storm — book and contributor biography
Black Eagle Books — Footprints of Fire

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bhaskaranand Jha Bhaskar writes in Maithili, Hindi and English, alongside short fiction, criticism and book reviews. His English poetry collections include Soothing Serenades: Straight from the Heart, Two Indias and Other Poems, and Thoughts in Solitude. His writing appears in Boloji and other literary journals; Setu has reviewed his collection of love poems, Soothing Serenades.

The poems gathered here seek renewal without denying hardship. “Life and Time” moves from a mind clouded by inertia towards the possibility of an awakened life. “Life is a Garden of Roses and Thorns” uses rhyming couplets to hold beauty and pain together, finding persistence in the flower that survives its prickles. Both poems turn familiar natural images into invitations to keep living attentively.

books.detail: English poetry · Authorspress, 2018 · Review in Setu

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bhaswati Basu’s Odia poems in Kabita Live give intimate speech a sharply questioning edge. In “ବୋଝ”, an inward burden is measured against Atlas’s sky, a broken wooden bird and the uneasy order of a room. The speaker’s eventual movement towards sunlight changes the poem from an account of hurt into an act of departure.

“କିଛି ଅମାନିଆ ପୁଅଙ୍କ ପାଇଁ” begins with a mother’s tenderness and turns towards a difficult question: can a son honour his own mother while denying dignity to other women? Repeated possibilities make the lullaby increasingly uneasy. Together, these poems examine the distance between the language of care and the way care is lived.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Bina Singh is a poet and teacher of English whose literary life is rooted in Varanasi. She formerly headed the English department at Vasant Kanya Mahavidyalaya. Her writing includes the poetry collection Jhanvi Keeps Me Afloat, and her editorial work includes Redemptive Musings, a bilingual anthology published by Hawakal.

The two poems collected here approach longing in different registers. “May Flower” lets scent and spring bloom awaken desire, then leaves the speaker uncertain whether the encounter was a dream. “Keshav, I am Lost” turns towards Krishna through images of dark woods, blocked paths and enduring faith. Sensuous attention and devotional address give these poems distinct ways of asking to be answered.

books.title: Redemptive Musings
books.detail: Edited anthology · English and Hindi poetry · Hawakal, 2019

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Chaitali Sengupta writes poetry, fiction and nonfiction and translates literature across languages. Her books include Cross-Stitched Words and The Crossings: Poems on War, Migration and Survival. Translation is another strand of her work, represented by Timeless Tales in Translation, which brings stories from Bengali and Hindi/Urdu into English.

Her Kabita Live poem “1971, Noakhali” follows a woman whose missing children and memories of violence cannot be contained by an official account of history. The poem moves through a Kolkata camp, knots in a sari and a torn kite, giving material form to what displacement leaves behind. Its broken, continuing sentences make remembrance feel both necessary and impossible to finish.

books.title: The Crossings: Poems on War, Migration and Survival
books.detail: English poetry · Hawakal, 2023 · Review in World Literature Today

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Chirashree Indrasingh writes Odia fiction and poetry and translates into Odia. Her translations include Bhalchandra Nemade’s Kosla, Jayanta Mahapatra’s Sky Without Sky and Namita Gokhale’s Things to Leave Behind. Her poetry collection Sadhi uses the sari to explore women’s lives; her story “Mother” also appears in the English-language anthology Spark of Light: Short Stories by Women Writers of Odisha.

In her poem here, the wish that someone far away should suffer less heat becomes a quiet measure of love. Television warnings, scorched flowers and an untouched bowl of water for birds bring the heatwave into a household. The poem’s dreamlike sun and half-burnt dream grow out of that physical landscape, making distance and tenderness part of the same weather.

books.title: Spark of Light: Short Stories by Women Writers of Odisha
books.detail: Contributing writer: “Mother” · Anthology · Athabasca University Press, 2016

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Chaitali Chattopadhyay is a Bengali poet from Kolkata whose writing also includes stories and essays. She studied physics and worked in advertising and magazines. Her first poetry collection, Bigyaponer Meye, appeared in 1988; a selection of her poems is available in English as Of Scars and Moonlight, translated by Bidisha Mukherjee.

“Afghanistan”, presented here in Shyamashri Ray Karmakar’s English translation, places a woman’s wish for sky, flowers and birds beside the sounds and traces of violence. Its brief movement from one enclosed life to a threatened world gives the title a widening significance. The poem’s fragile images of ordinary life remain visible even as its ending refuses reassurance.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Chittaranjan Mishra, also published as Chittaranjan Misra, is a poet, critic and translator working in Odia and English. He formerly headed the English department at B.J.B. Autonomous College in Bhubaneswar. His work includes the study Harold Pinter: The Dramatist and Odia translations of plays by Pinter and Albert Camus’s novel The Outsider.

In “ପ୍ରଥମ ଧାଡିରୁ”, words tremble, fall and survive like lives caught in the aftermath of disaster. The poem asks what language can retain when confronted with death, hunger and displacement. “ନିଃଶେଷ” narrows the scale to a remembered arrival and departure, leaving the spent stick of incense as an image of waiting. The public wound and the private absence both press against the limits of speech.

sources.label: The Antonym — Shadow and other poems

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Divya K Unni is the author of UnBridled, a poetry collection introduced at Bengaluru’s Atta Galatta in September 2025. Its poems move through love, belonging, loss and the wish for freedom. Her contributor biography also describes a background in teaching English and Hindi translation.

In “Time”, she addresses time as though it were a person free to make its own choices. The questions move from companionship to pleasure, pain and the length of a moment. Short, conversational lines keep the poem light on its feet while asking how freedom might change if we could choose when an experience ends.
