books.detail: Poetry collection · 2025 · Atta Galatta launch listing

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Devendra K Mishra writes poetry and fiction. His books include The Cursed Crow, Whenever I Feel and The Cara Coffee Bar. The latter follows university memories, friendship and an unexplained absence, while his poems also appear in literary spaces such as Primelore.

“Beaming Sorrows” condenses its landscape into brief, strongly sounded lines. Sun, river, wind, woods and birds take on the gestures of a troubled inner world. The quick movement of its images holds heat, weariness and grief together, ending with the unexpected suggestion that sorrow itself can shine.

sources.label: Zorba Books — The Cara Coffee Bar
Primelore — contributor poem and biography, April2026

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Devika Tripathy’s contributions to Kabita Live move between Hindi and English. Her Hindi poem “तू” builds its address through a repeated question, finding an enduring presence in the body, the cosmos and different places of worship. In “Moon”, the address becomes quieter: the moon keeps company with unspoken thoughts and a long night’s vigil.

“Where Love Lingers” and “Autumn Returning” stay with what remains after an encounter: music, pauses, remembered laughter and the ache of letting go. Small moments carry much of their emotional weight. Across these poems, repetition and direct address give longing a sustained, intimate voice.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Dilip Rakshit is a bilingual poet whose literary work sits alongside painting. A 2024 contributor biography in Literary Vibes places him in Durgapur, West Bengal, and describes his work teaching English literature privately. The journal also published his poems ‘Station’, ‘Reminiscence’ and ‘A Cup of Tea’.

In his Kabita Live poem ‘From core to zeal world’, enclosed spaces give way to an intensely coloured world. Pods, shells and the womb become images of containment and emergence, while light and the senses draw life outward. Cyan, green, gold and yellow recur through the poem, making colour part of its movement from inward darkness towards experience.

sources.label: Literary Vibes · Dilip Rakshit, poems and contributor biography · June 2024

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Deepika Dash’s Odia poems in Kabita Live move between intimate longing and the desire for freedom. In ‘ଲଜ୍ଜାଶୀଳା_ରୂପବତୀ’, moonlight, flowers, the sea and wandering wind seem to borrow their beauty and movement from the beloved. The landscape becomes a language for tenderness.

Her later poems shift the scale from a solitary star to a bird released from its cage. In ‘ଏକଲା_ତାରାର_ଲୁହ’, an apparent ending leaves behind a hopeful question; in ‘କେଡ଼େ କ୍ଷୁଦ୍ର ବ୍ରହ୍ମାଣ୍ଡ’, flight changes the bird’s sense of the world. These poems give small, vulnerable figures the power to imagine beyond their limits.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Dhananjay Kumar’s Hindi poem ‘विचारों की उड़ान’ treats thought as a form of travel. Its recurring image of flight carries the mind beyond familiar boundaries, through clouds, across rivers and into new dreams.

Repetition gives the poem its forward motion. Each return to the title phrase adds another possibility: creative energy, the spread of a message, the pursuit of knowledge or persistence through difficulty. The result is an invitation to keep the imagination moving.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Daipayan Nair is a poet from Silchar, Assam, working in Japanese short forms, including haiku, senryu and tanka. His writing appears in The Haiku Foundation’s Haiku Dialogue and in Yugen Quest Review. His collection ‘tilt of the winnowing fan’ was published by Hawakal in 2022.

The ten short poems gathered as ‘Haiku’ in Kabita Live attend to ordinary movement: a passenger leaving a puddle, a tea-seller opening milk, a boy spinning dough and a tea-plucker adjusting her bag. Weather, labour and small creatures share the same close field of attention. A raindrop gains weight beside ants; a grandfather’s knee becomes a landscape for an insect.

sources.label: Yugen Quest Review · Six Senryu and contributor biography · June 2023
The Haiku Foundation · Haiku Dialogue: personification

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Divya Vats writes poetry alongside her work in parenting and personal development. In her public professional profile, she describes her association with Adith Aadvan Consultancy and her work as a parenting coach, counsellor and writer.

Her Hindi poem ‘हर एक सूर्यास्त की सुबह होगी’ approaches disappointment through images of renewal. A broken dream gives way to another dream; a closed door is answered by a new opening. The recurring movement from endings to beginnings gives this brief poem its reassuring rhythm, ending with the thought that what seems lost may return in another form.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Dola Dutta Roy writes fiction and poetry, with a background spanning teaching and advertising. A Literary Vibes contributor biography traces her work from Calcutta to teaching overseas, further study in the United States and a later return to India and J. Walter Thompson. Her novel ‘And the Echoes Within’, listed by Notion Press, follows a mother confronting the demands of caregiving and her own hopes.

Her Kabita Live poems bring private grief into contact with a wider world. ‘SAYING GOODBYE’ follows a daughter bereaved during a viral outbreak as ordinary life continues around her; ‘LANDSCAPE of the Homeless’ confronts the destruction of home and family by war. ‘NIRVANA’ turns inward, following an exhausted seeker through fear and restless searching towards a moment of solace.

sources.label: Literary Vibes · Dola Dutta Roy contributor biography · November 2024
Notion Press · And the Echoes Within

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Dipak Samantarai brings poetry, broadcasting and heritage work together. His career with All India Radio spanned more than three decades, and his literary work includes the Odia poetry collections ‘Chhai Aluara Pashakhela’, ‘Kanthalekha’ and ‘Shosa’. His profile on the Cuttack Heritage website also records his work as editor and translator of ‘Seven Horses’.

In ‘Troubled Dawn’, the ordinary promise of morning falters: the sky hesitates, birds wait and a mother reaches for sleep. The poem moves from these domestic rhythms to a microscopic, spiked presence whose laughter overwhelms human suffering. Its short lines give the unfolding scene a suspended, unsettled pace.

sources.label: Dipak Samantarai · literary and broadcasting profile

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Debendra Lal writes poetry in Odia. A 2022 contributor note in Lothlorien Poetry Journal identifies him as a lawyer who grew up in Kesinga, Odisha, and names his poetry books ‘Andhakshara’ and ‘Birodhavasa’. The journal published three of his poems in English translations by Pitambar Naik.

His two Kabita Live poems bring different pressures to bear on feeling. ‘ବିପ୍ଳବ’ uses repeated calls to wait as a bitter irony: resistance is postponed while humiliation and loss accumulate. ‘କେବେକେବେ’ moves towards tears, imagining suffering in a child, an elderly person, a labouring body and even animals. Its final turn also makes room for tears of gratitude.

sources.label: Lothlorien Poetry Journal · Debendra Lal, translated by Pitambar Naik · September 2022

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Debajani Tripathy (1970–2025) was an Odia poet whose life connected Odisha and Idaho Falls in the United States. Born in Cuttack and educated in Bhubaneswar, she earned master’s degrees in sociology and education at Utkal University. Her obituary remembers her poetry alongside painting, gardening and an association with the Utkal Literature Festival.

In ‘ଗୋଟେ ପାଗେଳିର ପ୍ରେମ କବିତା’, love arrives as a conversation with oneself. Sleeplessness and everyday distractions give way to the image of a lamp persisting through darkness. The speaker repeatedly asks whether this enduring presence is love, illusion or belief, allowing uncertainty to remain part of the poem’s intimacy.

sources.label: Wood Funeral Home · Debajani (Panda) Tripathy obituary

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Diptirekha Das writes poetry in Odia and English and also works as a blogger. Her Literary Vibes contributor biography places her in Bhubaneswar and records postgraduate study in economics at Utkal University. The journal published ‘Healing Is Not Linear!’ and ‘The Forgotten Spring’, poems concerned with loss and the changing natural world.

Her Kabita Live poems ask what relationships need in order to endure. ‘The Pain Of Unsaid Words’ urges attention to people before the chance to listen is lost. ‘Don’t Set The Rules For Her’ shifts towards trust and personal freedom, ending with an image of flight and return. Together they place care alongside the need to leave another person room to breathe.

sources.label: Literary Vibes · Diptirekha Das, poems and biography · April 2023

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Debajani Ray’s Odia poems in Kabita Live explore the longing for fulfilment and the effort to begin again. ‘ସମୟ ର ବିଳାପ’ moves through love, belonging, identity and loss, drawing on stars, clouds, seasons and remembered cultural figures to give shape to a restless search.

In ‘ନିଷ୍ପତି’, discarded dreams and wounded hopes are gathered up rather than abandoned. Tears, moonlight, a courtyard and the sound of anklets turn the poem towards renewal through imagination. Its final movement lets poetry become a place where regret can find another voice.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Dilip Mohapatra is a poet and former Indian Navy commodore. His writing career reaches back to the 1970s, and his collections include A Pinch of Sun & Other Poems and Different Shades, published by Authorspress. A publisher’s profile places this literary life alongside a career in naval service and corporate leadership.

His Kabita Live poems often question the roles people are expected to play. ‘Reclusion’ follows the cost of self-effacement, while ‘Joker in the Pack’ turns a playing card into an image of identity shaped by others. In ‘Lost and Found’, the difficulties of ageing give way to the fellowship of a reunion; ‘Dots and Dashes’ finds value in life’s interruptions and imperfections.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Eli Mohanty’s ‘ମାଟି ରଂଗର ଭୋକ’, published in Kabita Live’s July 2024 edition, places hunger at the centre of a restless, questioning landscape. Earth, grain, a chariot wheel and the body recur as the speaker moves between material need and the language of ritual.

The poem’s images widen from the field to the cosmos, but keep returning to the hungry body. Its questions resist easy consolation: myth and prayer remain answerable to the need for food. This is a reading of the poem’s concerns, rather than an account of the poet’s personal life.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Eva Petropoulou-Lianou is a Greek writer from Xylokastro whose work includes poetry and books for children. Her published biography also describes her involvement in bringing Greek poets to wider literary audiences.

Her poems in Kabita Live speak directly to the reader. ‘Fallen Angel’ addresses people hurt by bullying or damaging relationships, asking them to recover their sense of worth and their capacity to help others. ‘Sun’ finds a gentler image for generosity in sunlight itself. Together, the poems place compassion in everyday acts of attention, encouragement and care.

sources.label: Academy of Ethics — Eva Petropoulou Lianou

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Elanaaga is a Telugu poet, translator and paediatrician whose work moves between Telugu and English. His writing includes metrical and experimental poetry as well as literary translation. He received the Sahitya Akademi Translation Prize for 2023 for Ghalib Naati Kaalam, his Telugu translation of Pavan K. Varma’s biography Ghalib: The Man, The Times.

In his Kabita Live poems, moral questions become vivid, sometimes unsettling images. ‘The Awaited Arrival’ addresses impartiality as an absent presence, while ‘Inner Embers’ measures war through the suffering of ordinary people. ‘Quagmire of Confusion’ turns inward, tracing the way anger and distorted perception can unsettle both thought and language.

sources.label: Episteme, June 2017 — Closed Doors and Other Poems

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Eileen Moynihan writes children’s books, poetry and short stories. Born in Essex and raised on the Isle of Wight, she moved to Ireland as a young adult. Her author biography describes a career teaching children with special needs, followed by writing and publishing under the names Childhood Books and Landscape Books.

‘A Child Again’, her contribution to Kabita Live, finds renewal in an outing with a granddaughter at Wellington’s Botanic Gardens. Cicadas, ducks and small discoveries carry the poem forward, while the child’s delight in words changes how the adult sees the day. The poem makes intergenerational companionship a way of recovering curiosity.

sources.label: Eileen Moynihan — March 2023 author blog, syndicated on Goodreads

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ganeswar Behera is a bilingual poet associated with Jajpur, Odisha, according to his Kabita Live contributor note. His two poems here, ‘Spiral thoughts’ and ‘GINGERY CARE’, explore affection through the unsettled language of longing.

Both poems address an absent or distant beloved. Heartbeats, whispers and imagined embraces become ways of holding a relationship close, even as restless thoughts interrupt that wish. Their short stanzas and intimate forms of address give emotional uncertainty a conversational voice.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gayatri Mavuru is a poet, artist, educator and translator. Her collection Sizzling Verses: Drizzling Colours appears in the Guntur International Poetry Festival’s record of book releases. Outlook has also published her English translation of Tirupati Kiran’s Telugu story ‘Lives in the Shadows’.

In ‘The Burden of Creation’, her poem in Kabita Live, artistic work becomes both a struggle and a source of renewal. Pigment, canvas, brushstroke and clay give physical form to doubt and persistence. The repeated act of carrying gathers failures and moments of wonder into the same life, moving towards a quiet reconciliation between the maker and what is made.

sources.label: Guntur International Poetry Festival — Books released

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gayatri Das writes in Odia and English and is from Anugul, Odisha, according to her Kabita Live contributor note.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gopikrishnan Kottoor is an Indian poet whose work also includes drama, translation and literary editing. He founded the poetry journal Poetry Chain and edited A New Book of Poems in English. His contributor note in Shot Glass Journal records appearances in Best Asian Poetry, Acumen and Nth Position.

His collection A Land in the Sun, published by Penprints, offers an entry into a body of work concerned with love, loss, nature and ordinary experience. The publisher highlights poems such as ‘My Father’s Shirt’ and ‘The Last Man in the Bar’. These are starting points in his wider published work; the current Kabita Live catalogue does not yet link a poem to this profile.

sources.label: Penprints — A Land in the Sun

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Goutam Jena’s ‘ସ୍ମିତହସ’, published in Kabita Live’s February 2024 edition, begins with a simple smile free of mockery or pretence. The poem gradually opens that image to many interpretations, comparing its power to connect feelings with a bridge across a river.

Light and shadow, retreating waves and a bird’s wings give that inquiry a changing landscape. Later passages question pride, self-deception and the difficulty of finding truth. The smile survives these doubts as something still fresh and elusive, renewing the poem’s search rather than settling it.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Geethanjali Dilip is a poet and French educator associated with Zone Francofone in Salem, Tamil Nadu. Her literary work includes collaborative anthologies and the curation of the Yercaud Poetry Festival. Her collections include Geethatmaa: Song of the Soul and Rosée: The Dewdrop.

The poems gathered here move between intimate connection and public grief. ‘Lines’ follows a relationship beyond telephone wires into the quiet language of touch. ‘When it all reflects’ brings together images of womanhood and the earth’s abundance, while ‘Wasted Penance’ questions the human cost hidden beneath war songs, medals and patriotic ceremony.

sources.label: Sujatha Warrier — Book launch at Mysuru

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gayatree G Lahon is a poet and teacher from Assam. Her contributor biographies record postgraduate study in English literature at Gauhati University and publication in literary journals and anthologies, including GloMag and Our Poetry Archive.

In ‘Trees Sing’, her poem in Kabita Live, listening becomes a way of recovering an inner life. Leaves, breeze and imagined song answer the speaker’s numbness, while the poem questions a world too occupied with possessions to hear either nature or itself. Its movement from emptiness towards solace rests on quiet, attentive observation.

sources.label: Our Poetry Archive — Gayatree G Lahon, May2019

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Garima Garg is a poet and translator associated with Panchkula, Haryana. Alongside her Hindi poems, her work includes bringing Pradeep Biswal’s poetry into Punjabi. The Pioneer reported the release of that translation, published by Shalandi Books, at the Toshali Literature Festival in February 2023.

Her two poems in Kabita Live approach language as a means of connection and agency. ‘एहसास’ moves through appeals for humane conversation, care for the earth and relief from sorrow. ‘कलम हथियार लायी हूँ’ gives the pen a sharp edge without losing tenderness: its speaker brings feeling, colour and the fragrance of flowers into the act of writing.

sources.label: The Pioneer — Odia poet Biswal’s works in Punjabi released, February15 2023

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gargi Saha is a poet whose collections include The Muse in My Salad Days (2000) and Letters to Him (2012). Reviewing the latter, Ramesh Anand describes its linked poems as an extended dialogue of prayer, questioning and gratitude. Her poetry has also appeared in Literary Vibes.

Her Kabita Live contributions find expressive possibilities in everyday sights and sounds. ‘Onomatopoeia’ gathers a world of rustling, humming and calls, while ‘The Simple Pleasures of Life’ attends to birds, rain and green landscapes. ‘Ineffable Altruism’ asks what people owe the earth that feeds them; ‘Withdrawal’ turns towards isolation and remembered happiness. These contrasting poems place delight beside vulnerability.

sources.label: Boloji — Ramesh Anand reviews Letters to Him

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gopa Bhattacharjee is a bilingual poet and entrepreneur from Kolkata. Her English collections include Unturned Verses and Thirty Birds. Her literary activity also includes interviewing fellow writers: in IPPL Journal, she speaks with Lopamudra Banerjee about poetry, collaboration and translation.

Her poems in Kabita Live explore moments when an inner voice confronts loss or resistance. ‘Transient’ brings sleeplessness, memory and winter into a brief recognition of impermanence. ‘The Soliloquy’ draws on Shakespearean figures and a phoenix image to move from betrayal and doubt towards renewed courage.

sources.label: IPPL Journal — Interview with Lopamudra Banerjee, April2024

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gopa Nayak writes poetry in English and Odia and translates Odia literature into English. Raised in Bhubaneswar, she pursued postgraduate study at Oxford, earning a DPhil. Her poetry collection Dissension appeared in 2011; her writing brings language, memory and the experience of living across cultures into conversation.

In Kabita Live, ‘Illusion’ asks whether love can be dismissed as unreal when taste, scent and touch make it so vividly present. ‘Shakuntala’ turns to a different kind of remembering: a woman speaks through the roles assigned to her by myth, questioning abandonment and insisting on her own account of motherhood and identity.

sources.label: Gopa Nayak — contributor biography, Times of India

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gourhari Das writes across poetry, short fiction, novels, essays and drama, and translates into Odia. His short-story collection Kanta O Anyanya Galpa received the Sahitya Akademi Award in 2012. His Odia translation of Benyamin’s Goat Days, Chheli Chareibara Dina, received the Akademi’s translation award for 2021. The Labyrinth brings his fiction to English readers in Manoranjan Mishra’s translation.

His poem ‘ଗୋଟେ ସମୟରେ, ଏଇ ପୃଥିବୀରେ’ gives love a quieter measure than reunion. Through flowers, remembered roads and the distance between two lives, it finds value in having shared a time on earth. Its returning phrases hold that recognition gently, even when society and circumstance keep the lovers apart.

books.title: The Labyrinth
books.detail: Novel · translated from Odia by Manoranjan Mishra · Niyogi Books

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Gopal Lahiri is a bilingual poet, critic, editor and translator. His collection Anemone Morning and Other Poems was published by Penprints in 2024. Alongside his books, his poems appear in literary journals including Setu, which recognised him with its poetry excellence award in 2020.

His Kabita Live poems linger over small signs of life. ‘Flame’ looks closely at an ageing woman, finding vitality within physical frailty. In ‘Walkway’, flowers, bees and sunlight pass from one short stanza into the next through repeated phrases. That linked movement lets a simple path unfold as a sequence of discoveries.

sources.label: Gopal Lahiri — Setu special edition and contributor biography
Anemone Morning — review by Malashri Lal, Setu

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Heba Fatima writes poetry and literary criticism. Her published work identifies her as an English lecturer at Birupa College in Odisha, with interests in folklore, gender and popular culture. Her essay ‘The Reptile Within’ studies how contemporary Odia short stories revisit a Panchatantra fable; her criticism also includes a review of Steven Feld’s work on sound, song and mourning.

In Kabita Live, ‘Abandoned Homes’ makes domestic ruins and broken toys bear the weight of displacement and loss. ‘To My Velutha’ turns inward, addressing an absent beloved through images of water, memory and a grief that keeps growing. Both poems ask what remains of home when the people or future that gave it meaning are threatened.

sources.label: Heba Fatima — Sound and Sentiment review, Northeast Popular Culture Association
The Reptile Within — journal article by Heba Fatima

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Haimanti Dutta Ray writes poetry and prose. Her books include In Loving Memory, published in 2015, and The Circle of Life & Other Tales, published in 2018. In her own essay about her father, the painter Shyamal Dutta Ray, intimate recollections of family life sit beside an account of the artistic world she grew up around.

‘Herald in the Chill’, her poem in Kabita Live, welcomes winter with flowers, birds, woollens and cups of tea. Its literary allusions share space with aching bones and the pleasure of ice cream in cold weather. The result is an affectionate, lightly humorous invitation to find renewal in the season’s ordinary comforts.

sources.label: Haimanti Dutta Ray — Of This & That: Reliving Memories of Shyamal Duttaray

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Himanshu Parida’s work in Kabita Live spans Odia and English poetry. His interest in the craft of writing also finds a place in Metaphor O Ehara Upajogita, an Odia book published by Pakshighar Prakashanee.

‘ଅଚିର’ sets the poet’s impulse to build and repair against the slow undoing of bodies, buildings and memorials. ‘My Mother’s Death’ approaches loss through the practical details of a household: a stopped newspaper, an empty chair, cancelled visits and food left over. The ordinary routine continues, making the absence within it all the more palpable.

sources.label: Metaphor O Ehara Upajogita — Ritikart book listing

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Haraprit Kaur’s Hindi poem ‘काश’ appears in Kabita Live’s February 2023 edition. Its repeated wish opens outward from a world without borders to daughters living without fear, families finding one another beyond their screens, and a society free of inherited divisions.

The poem moves between the intimate and the collective: the distance within a home matters alongside the boundaries between communities. Each return to ‘काश’ gives that longing a fresh starting point, ending with the hope of the world becoming one family.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Hiranmayee Mishra writes poetry and fiction in Odia alongside research on gender and public life. Her University of York doctoral study examined how women in Odisha’s village councils negotiate the barriers between family responsibilities and political participation. In an interview about her literary work, she described relationships and gender justice as subjects that draw her to fiction.

Her poem ‘ଧୋତି’ brings that attention to a household transformed by bereavement. The remembered colour of a mother’s sari, bangles and sindoor gives way to the white cloth imposed on her as a widow. Through the speaker’s shock and anger, the poem questions customs that turn grief into a further loss of dignity and freedom.

sources.label: Hiranmayee Mishra — doctoral thesis, University of York / White Rose
Gender justice themes attract me — author interview, OrissaPOST

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Himanshu Jena, also published as Himanshu Bhushan Jena, is a bilingual poet from Raipur in Odisha’s Jajpur district. His collections include Tranquil Rapture, Spring of Serenity and Ripples of Reflection. The last was published by Booksclinic Publishing in 2020.

His Kabita Live poems use fire, flowers and light to speak about integrity and purposeful action. ‘Walking in Fire’ imagines resolve as a force that can answer difficult circumstances. ‘Body, the Catalyst for Supreme Alchemy’ and ‘Staying True to Oneself’ turn to the relationship between the mortal body and an enduring inner life, measuring that life through conduct and concern for humanity.

books.title: Ripples of Reflection: A Florilegium of Poems

sources.label: Being Human — Inner Child Press contributor biography
Ripples of Reflection — Google Books bibliographic record

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Hardaman Singh is a poet with longstanding ties to Bhubaneswar. In a personal essay for My City Links, he recalls arriving in the city as a child and growing up among its changing streets, schools and neighbourhoods. His published books include Crossroads and Mirrored Reflections.

‘The Old Album’, his poem in Kabita Live, holds memory in the small movements of hands and faces. Faded photographs bring a glint to ageing eyes and a smile to worn lips. Its brief paired lines slow the reader to the pace of someone turning an album’s pages, letting affection survive where the images themselves are wearing away.

sources.label: My City My Pride — personal essay by Hardaman Singh, My City Links

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Harinder Cheema is a poet and author whose books include The Temple Stop and Soul Chants. In an interview about her writing, she spoke of literature’s relationship with society and of the need to look beyond personal gain towards a shared good.

‘At the Time of Homecoming’, her poem in Kabita Live, imagines earthly life as a school day and the Creator as a parent waiting at home. Its familiar images of play, rules and a clean uniform frame a moral question: what kind of life will we have lived when it is time to return?

sources.label: Harinder Cheema — author interview, Polis Magazino

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Inam Hussain Begg Mullick is a Kolkata poet and editor whose creative work also includes photography, music and performance. His poetry collections include Roses for the Madhouse, Winter’s Electric Architecture and The Magical Life of Inamorato, published by Writers Workshop in 2021. His work has appeared in literary journals including Usawa.

In ‘The Kingdom of Golden Dreams’, his Kabita Live poem, the city repeatedly opens into an imagined landscape. A diving cormorant, a rag-picker lifting clouds and flowers blooming among wounds bring beauty into contact with loss. Across six sections, past and present return to one another through dream, music and remembered affection.

sources.label: The Magical Life of Inamorato — Writers Workshop
A Couplet — poetry and contributor biography, Usawa

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ipsita Ganguli writes poetry and travel prose and takes an active interest in heritage and the arts. Her books include Of Love, Longing and Random Pondering and Rooted, India 75, and We the People. Alongside her writing, she has curated poetry events and developed literary conversations for audiences in Kolkata and online.

‘Blissfully Yours’, her poem in Kabita Live, imagines togetherness carried by clouds, rain, birds and a gentle breeze. The lovers build a shared heaven, then release it to the wind. Affection here becomes most sustaining when it allows freedom rather than possession.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ipsita Sarangi is an Odia poet, critic and translator. In a literary interview, she described growing up with poetry and finding particular satisfaction in translating it across languages. Her translation work includes stories by Sarojini Sahoo and an Odia version of Kedarnath Singh’s Bagha.

In ‘ସମୟ’, her Kabita Live poem, time becomes a presence the speaker questions, seeking a way through uncertainty, wounded existence and elusive words. ‘Girls without Tongues’, presented in Bandana Sahoo’s English translation from Odia, turns towards girls burdened with adult responsibilities and denied a sense of belonging. Its images of embers and water hold together the pressure of silence and the hope of a fuller life.

sources.label: Ipsita Sarangi — interview by Ramakrishna Perugu, Together, October 2025
Sorrows Unending — Sarojini Sahoo’s author blog

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Juya Tripathy’s Odia poem ‘ପ୍ରେମ’ appears in Kabita Live’s July 2026 edition. It answers the idea that love belongs only to youth or bodily desire by imagining a beloved’s arrival at the very end of life.

The speaker waits beyond fading sight and physical strength for a touch and a kiss on a wrinkled forehead. With the images of Ganga water and a final embrace, the poem brings tenderness into conversation with mortality and spiritual release.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jyotirmaya Thakur writes poetry in English and Hindi, alongside fiction, essays and drama. A retired school educator, she is the author of Musings of a Mystic: Metaphysical Verses, published by Clever Fox in 2020, and the Hindi poetry collection Talaash.

In “When We Gather at the Rivers,” a remembered maternal hymn opens onto the Ganga, worship and the struggle to protect a place for faith. The poem moves from childhood recollection to public argument, returning finally to water and reflected aarti flames as images of an inward sanctuary.

books.title: Musings of a Mystic: Metaphysical Verses

sources.label: Google Books — Musings of a Mystic

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Johny Takkedasila is a Telugu poet, fiction writer, critic and translator from Pulivendula, Andhra Pradesh, whose writing also spans Hindi and English. His Telugu critical work Vivechani received the Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar in 2023. His books include Nadaka, published by Ukiyoto.

In “Sometimes I Freeze,” emotional paralysis becomes stone, wounded breath and a body struggling to move. Blood, tears, fire and rain carry the poem through a series of transformations, until its closing address joins pain with gratitude toward the person who sets the speaker in motion.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Julie Miles’s “August for Jamie” returns to the month of its title as a measure of enduring love. Rain, soil, breath and a river of tears give grief a physical presence, while the repeated arrival of August sets calendar time against a bond that does not fade.

The poem also questions the rituals and language of anniversaries: whether their familiar words can reach the depth of remembrance. Its direct address to Jamie keeps that question intimate, ending with a presence felt in August and beyond it.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jay Jagdev, also known as JP Jagdev, brings together entrepreneurship, research and literary work. His own website gathers poems and essays, while his work with the Udaygiri Foundation connects him to the literary life of Odisha; a participant’s account of the 2025 Toshali Literature Festival identifies him as the foundation’s president.

“My Desires” turns longing into a sequence of contradictions: solitude becomes companionship, darkness a way of seeing, and absence a means of preserving the beloved. The final contrast between a portrait held in the heart and a troubled memory gives the poem its quiet tension.

sources.label: Dewan Sastera — participant account of Toshali 2025

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jyosthnarani Bhoi’s Odia poem “ଆଖି ତଳ କଳାରେ” begins with sleeplessness and the marks it leaves beneath the eyes. A layer of powder over suffering skin sets outward appearance against an inward hurt that cannot so easily be hidden.

The poem then turns toward earth: the ground on which one stands and learns to take root. Its closing insistence that the feet must be one’s own gives this movement from bodily weariness to rootedness a sense of self-reliance.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jyoti Nanda is an Odia fiction writer, poet, essayist and translator. His books include the story collection Pingala Panjuri and the novel Pakshijanma. In a 2019 interview with Saroj Bal, he describes a growing understanding of fiction as social work, alongside his continuing interest in experiments with narrative form.

In “ବିପଜ୍ଜନକ ପ୍ରେମ କବିତା,” the lives of two labourers interrupt the polished language of poetry and the city’s confidence in progress. Road trenches, buried cables, loss and a proposed magic act converge in a question about what people are willing to see. Its love is inseparable from the insecurity and grief of working lives.

sources.label: Odisha Sambad — Saroj Bal interviews Jyoti Nanda, 2019

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jagari Mukherjee is a poet and editor whose collections include The Elegant Nobody (Hawakal, 2020) and Exit Noire (BookWryter, 2023). The Elegant Nobody was shortlisted for the Rabindranath Tagore Literary Prize for 2021–22. She is also associated with the literary journal EKL Review as its Chief Executive Editor.

“My Sister and I Comb a Doll’s Hair” begins with the bright colours and careful gestures of play. Its final disclosure—that the sisters are childless, middle-aged women—turns attention toward the reader’s expectations. The doll’s silence holds a tenderness that resists easy explanation or judgment.

sources.label: World Literature Today — verse review index
Setu — Gopal Lahiri reviews The Elegant Nobody

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jinatamam Darji’s Odia poems in Kabita Live bring public violence and private vulnerability into the same field of vision. In “ମାଷ୍ଟର ମାଇଣ୍ଡ,” territorial conflict and a wounded dove lead toward a poet who recognises the hidden figure behind destruction. “ଅସମୟ” asks what kind of world would allow a girl to grow up, play and move freely without fear.

Trees and the earth offer another language for change. “ପତ୍ରଝଡା ଋତୁ” imagines the transformations of the Buddha and Valmiki through the shedding of leaves; in “ପୁନର୍ଣ୍ଣବା,” the earth casts off the wounds left by oppressive power and announces renewal. Across these poems, questions about conscience become vivid, physical scenes.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jaydeep Sarangi is a poet and literary scholar whose books include letters in lower case (Authorspress, 2022). His work has a close association with the river Dulung and its communities. Alongside his poetry, he has edited Teesta, a journal of poetry and criticism, and collaborated with Rob Harle on anthologies bringing Indian and Australian poets together.

The poems collected here approach landscape as an inward journey. “Road to a Different Person” turns Himalayan travel into an account of change; “Are You Watching Me?” moves through loneliness, rejection and sleeplessness toward an uncertain hope. Hills, running water and waiting tulip buds give these acts of questioning a tangible setting.

sources.label: Setu — Jaydeep Sarangi contributor biography, April2023
Indialogs — Basudhara Roy reviews letters in lower case

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jyoti Shankar Panda “Hayat” is represented here by the Hindi poem “गीतकवि की व्यथा,” a sustained address from a poet to the public. Its recurring plea for forgiveness measures artistic success against the suffering the speaker has failed to share.

Each stanza adds another thing imagined as sold: tears, love, truth, the self, light and finally the rights of others. The repeated return home contrasts private comfort with collective deprivation, turning the song into a searching argument about the responsibilities of writing.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jnani Debashis Mishra, also published as Jnanee Debasish Mishra, is an Odia poet and literary scholar associated with Ravenshaw University. His poetry collection Daaga received the Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar in 2016. His critical writing includes work on comparative literature, bringing the study of literary relationships alongside his own creative practice.

In “ବାଟଖୋଜା,” the river becomes a teacher of persistence, generosity and the search for a path. Its difficult journey toward the sea contrasts with lives spent choosing comfort. The poem’s later landscape of cement sharpens this contrast into an ecological warning, before returning to the possibility of a living spring within each person.

sources.label: Prachee article deposited in Zenodo — comparative literature

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jayanta Mahapatra (1928–2023) was a poet from Cuttack whose literary life grew alongside a career teaching physics. Writing in English and Odia, he also edited the literary journal Chandrabhaga. His collections include A Rain of Rites, published by the University of Georgia Press in 1976; he received the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1981.

In “Playing the Magician,” a newspaper report, a passing train and an animal’s death disturb the surface of an ordinary day. The poem moves between intimate perception and questions about the country’s conscience. Its shifting images resist an easy resolution: the observing mind remains entangled in the world it tries to understand.

sources.label: University of Hyderabad — memorial for Jayanta Mahapatra
Contemporary Poetry Review — conversation with Jayanta Mahapatra

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jayanti Rath’s writing spans Odia fiction, poetry and historical research. Her work in cultural institutions includes service as superintendent of the Odisha State Museum, where she took part in the launch of its online manuscript catalogue in 2014. Sahitya Akademi records her participation in Odia short-story readings and publishes her monograph on the historian Satya Narayana Rajguru.

In “ଅକ୍ଷର ଆଳାପ,” the difficulty of speaking becomes a difficulty of reading the world. A leafless tree laden with fruit, letters scattered through branches and sky, and a fading dream make an inward disquiet visible. The poem holds the speaker’s solitude against the lost intimacy of conversation with words.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jernail Singh Anand is a poet and prose writer from Punjab, and founder-president of the International Academy of Ethics. His writing includes the Mahakaal Trilogy and works of literary criticism. In an interview published by the academy, he describes literature as a way to bring ethical questions into ordinary life, and argues that books should reach people beyond academic discussion.

His Kabita Live poems approach those questions through familiar images. “MEMORIES” imagines the past as water we continue to inhabit, while a mind carries its stations even after a train has left them behind. “TRUTH: PARTIAL AND IMPARTIAL” sets poetry’s power to soothe and interpret against the violence and contested narratives of history. Together, they ask how language shapes what we remember and what we accept as true.

sources.label: International Academy of Ethics — interview with Jernail Singh Anand

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jyoti Jha writes fiction, poetry and travel narratives in English and Hindi. A former human-resources professional, she found a turning point in The Times of India’s Write India competition, later discussing that journey at Times LitFest. Her books include the Hindi novel Aanandi, the travel title Around the World Through My Lens and the short-story collection Heart’s Sanctuary & Other Stories.

“Hues of Nature” gathers its movement from colour and light: blue sky, green foliage, grey shadow and golden rays. The quiet scene opens into a reflection on solitude and purpose, letting sensory attention become a way of looking inward. Her author website also records the poem’s appearance in the Toshali Anthology of Poetry, connecting this Kabita Live contribution with her wider poetry publication.

sources.label: Times of India — Jyoti Jha at Times LitFest
Google Books — Heart’s Sanctuary & Other Stories

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Jayantika is the literary name of Jayanti Panda, an Odia poet who taught political science. In a personal recollection, fellow writer Pradeep Biswal traces her teaching career from Vyasanagar College to government colleges and her retirement as a reader at JKBK College in Cuttack. Her Kabita Live biography records her continued dedication to creative writing after retirement.

“ନିରକ୍ଷରା” questions what it means to be unable to read. Its eyes understand joy, loss and tenderness beyond the reach of grammar, while an impatient world mistrusts such sensitivity. The closing uncertainty over whose heartbeat is being heard makes intimacy itself a form of understanding.

sources.label: Pradeep Biswal — Dash Benhur: A Dedicated Writer

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kallol Choudhury works across poetry, short fiction and translation. Sahitya Akademi published Samparka, his Bengali translation of Jayanta Mahapatra’s Relationship, in 2006. His English poetry collection Buddha on Planchette was published by Penprints in 2023; his publisher also records contributions of stories, translations and a folktale to Oxford University Press anthologies.

The two poems gathered here turn affection into a landscape of colour and touch. “The Bluish Splendour Of Your Eyes” moves between brightness and passing gloom, finding transformation in an artistic hand. In “In The Moonlight Soaked Meadow,” afternoon, dusk and river become ways of remembering a face. The river’s movement carries the tenderness that the speaker tries to hold.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Krushna Kumar Mohanty writes poetry, short stories and essays in Odia. His books include the story collection Shyamali Das and Ruby Ray, a poetry collection published by Timepass in 2023. A notice in Srujan: The Creativity Journal also records his editorial work with Rebatee, placing his own writing alongside an involvement in the wider literary community.

In “ବନ୍ଧନୀ,” a repeated declaration of arrival is shadowed by the question of whether the past can really be left behind. Memory becomes a safety pin holding a torn mind together; later, forests appear like temples and the path itself begins to yield love poetry. The movement toward another person carries both vulnerability and the possibility of renewal.

sources.label: Srujan: The Creativity Journal — Ruby Ray book notice, 2023

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kanak Manjari Sahoo is an Odia short-story writer and translator whose work brings Bengali and Hindi literature to Odia readers. Her author biography lists the story collection Ashtaraga alongside translations of Zakir Hussain and Sunil Gangopadhyay, as well as collections of folktales. Sahitya Akademi’s catalogue records her translation of Laghu Katha Sangrah, adding a documented title to this wider practice of carrying stories between languages.

Her brief poem “The wheels of time have run over them” presents a traveller who has not yet reached the hoped-for destination. Obstacles remain, but the movement continues. Time, first imagined as something that can crush, opens into sky and fields around the path: an unfinished journey held within a spacious landscape.

sources.label: Kanak Manjari Sahoo — author biography and bibliography

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kumudini Jee’s poems in Kabita Live turn familiar images into questions about attachment and self-understanding. In “ଫାଶ,” the speaker watches a trapped dove struggle to escape, while recognising an opposing wish to cast a snare. The final reversal unsettles the boundary between caring for another and wanting to possess them.

“ଅଙ୍କ କଷା” gives inward reckoning the language of mathematics. Algebra and trigonometry meet a bird’s flight, sunset and the marks of grief, but no simple calculation can contain them. The poem’s search is for a whole self that can hold these scattered experiences together.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kavita Singh Prava writes in Hindi and is based in Delhi, according to her Kabita Live biography. Her poem “कठपुतलियाँ” brings questions of pride, impermanence and human agency into a direct, recurring address.

The image of puppets in time’s hands returns like a refrain, stripping away the distinctions between beggar and king. Yet the poem does not end in resignation: it asks the reader to break the cage of ego and leave a mark through action. What remains, it suggests, is the work one has done rather than the name one has carried.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ketaki Mazumdar is a poet and educationist based in Mumbai, with childhood roots in Kolkata. Her poetry collections include Woodsmoke and Embers and Toasted Orange Embers. In an interview with The Wise Owl, she describes resilience, empathy and healing as concerns that draw her poems together, and close observation of colour and movement as part of her writing practice.

In Kabita Live’s ‘Holding On Letting Go’, grief and uncertainty are met through small acts of attention: flowering trees, an earthen lamp, a river and birdsong. The poem moves between vulnerability and wonder, finding renewal without pretending that loss has disappeared.

books.title: Toasted Orange Embers
books.detail: Poetry · author interview in The Wise Owl

sources.label: The Wise Owl — Talking Books with Ketaki Mazumdar

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: K. V. Dominic is an Indian English poet, fiction writer, critic and editor whose literary work grew alongside a career teaching English at Newman College in Thodupuzha, Kerala. His author biography records his retirement in 2011 and his earlier editorship of the Indian Journal of Postcolonial Literatures. Winged Reason is among his poetry collections.

His poems in Kabita Live bring questions of justice into everyday scenes. ‘Equity must begin at home’ challenges unequal treatment of women, while ‘On War and Peace’ asks readers to imagine suffering beyond their own borders. ‘Advent of Monsoon’ sets the beauty of rain against the danger it brings to vulnerable households. In ‘Bunyan Tree: Happy New Year’, a sheltering tree questions the distance between festive greetings and care for other lives.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kajal Chaudhury is introduced in her Kabita Live biography as a poet writing in Hindi and English. Her Hindi poems here approach love through freedom, tenderness and the things that cannot be demanded from another person.

In ‘ग़ज़ल’, mist, fragrance and rain give shape to affection that arrives without force or possession. ‘रजनीगंधा’ takes that thought into a quieter exchange: ornaments that might bind are set aside in favour of flowers and their fragrance. Read together, the poems imagine closeness as something that leaves the inner life free.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kumudini Ved is a Mumbai-based poet and artist whose creative interests include painting, music and writing. Rhyvers Beat published her poem ‘Pouring Rain, Steaming Coffee’ in its February 2023 issue. Her collection Kinetic Konnections — The Poetry We Live brings together poetry in several languages, extending the multilingual practice described in her Kabita Live biography.

In her Kabita Live poem ‘DUSK’, the changing light becomes a richly coloured presence: fiery clothing gives way to velvet darkness, while a lone bird, still water and prayer bells mark the passage into night. Beneath this beauty lies the pressure of unfulfilled dreams. The poem holds that weariness alongside the possibility of another dawn.

sources.label: The Prime India — Kumudini Ved book launch

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kavita Singh writes under the pen name ‘Prabha’ and works across Hindi poetry, ghazals, songs and theatre. An educator, she describes directing plays and creating dance dramas for children as part of her creative life. Her author website brings teaching and literary practice together through poems, performances and work promoting Hindi.

Her Kabita Live poems turn inward feelings into direct appeals to the reader. ‘क्रोध’ asks for restraint and compassion in the face of anger; ‘इंतज़ार’ gives voice to parents waiting for their grown children to return. In ‘यह तृषा है!’, thirst becomes a wider image of human longing, capable of both disturbing the heart and sustaining its dreams.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kakoli Ghosh writes poetry in English and Bengali and also paints. Published under her name and as ‘Moon Drops’, her work appears in literary journals and international anthologies. GloMag’s contributor note identifies her collections Unfinished and The Bridge, connecting the poet’s literary work with her interest in visual art.

In Kabita Live, her poems give loneliness and memory a physical presence. ‘The Water Of Life’ draws on distilling, bottles and wine stains to explore grief that outlasts attempts to contain it. ‘Slipping into something else’ moves through emptied spaces, ripening fields, flooded nests and bodily images, making change feel at once intimate and unsettling.

sources.label: Poetry for Ukraine — Kakoli Ghosh, page 256

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kedar Mishra is an Odia poet, translator, editor and art critic from Sonepur. His work extends into journalism and writing on classical dance and music. His poetry collections include Raga Kedar and Premara Dura Geeta; the Kalinga Literary Festival also records his work as a scriptwriter for Odissi performances.

In ‘ଆଖି : ସତ୍ୟାଗ୍ରହ’, his Kabita Live contribution, a beloved’s eyes become a refuge amid images of war, tears and defeat. The poem draws on the Mahabharata’s dice game and eighteen-day battle, then moves towards shelter, love and nonviolent resistance. Its intimate address allows tenderness and protest to inhabit the same poem.

books.title: This Country Is Not Mine
books.detail: Poetry · book review by Rabindra Swain

sources.label: OdishaBytes — Rabindra Swain on This Country Is Not Mine

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kaberi Chattopadhyaya, published as Kaberi Chattopadhyay, grew up in Assam and taught English in West Bengal. Her writing includes the memoir Peeping Through My Window, the poetry collection The Twilight Bells and short fiction. Her publisher’s account connects an education at Calcutta University and North Eastern Hill University with a teaching career at Ramkrishna Vivekananda Mission and Army Public School, Barrackpore.

Her Kabita Live poems often pause at moments when a life changes its shape. ‘The silver bathed night’ observes a father facing retirement; ‘DUKHIRAM’ discovers a labouring boy’s lost childhood in a kaleidoscope. ‘Love`s First Rays’ attends to an unexpected awakening of affection, while ‘AS LIFE DEMANDS’ turns towards the ethical choices people make in a world of unequal joys and sorrows.

sources.label: Penprints — Apparitions from the Other World

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Kamadev Moharana is an Odia poet and fiction writer whose imagination is rooted in the rivers and coast around Astarang. In an interview with Odisha Sambad, he recalls the landscape of his childhood in Badagola and the books that drew him towards literature. His collections include Kabi, Chhai Saha Sabudina and Coffee Bagicha. He describes poetry as a witness to the social and cultural life of its time.

His Kabita Live poems bring that relationship between place and people into focus. ‘ଘନ ବେହେରାର ଗୀତ’ follows a fisherman into darkness, carrying a mother’s warning, the demands of home and an epic song towards the sea. ‘ସେମାନେ କହୁଥିବା ଏକ ନଷ୍ଟ ସ୍ଵର୍ଗର ଫଟୋଚିତ୍ର’ remembers a river, banyan tree and village gathering place as a shared world gradually damaged and lost. Landscape here holds both livelihood and communal memory.

sources.label: Odisha Sambad — Supriya Panda interviews Kamadev Moharana, 29 August 2021

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Ketaki Datta is a poet, novelist, translator and literary reviewer with a background in teaching English in Kolkata. Her writing moves between original fiction and poetry, literary criticism and translation. Her collections include Across the Blue Horizon and The Music of Eternity; Urban Reflections brings her poems into conversation with Wilfried Raussert’s photographs.

In her Kabita Live poem ‘Pinpointing the emotions’, she asks whether anguish can be located as precisely as a chamber of the heart. The questions widen into the distinctions between loneliness and solitude, waiting and endurance. Autumn leaves, birds, still water and trembling dew carry the poem back towards remembered days of celebration.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Lopamudra Singh writes poetry and engages with literature through reading and reviewing. Her contributor note in Literary Vibes describes a background in electrical engineering and work in Odisha’s Commercial Tax and GST administration. The journal has published her poems ‘The City’s Amnesia’ and ‘The Unknowing Void’.

Her Kabita Live poem ‘A Carefree Drift’ imagines an escape into sunshine, mist, waterfalls and wildflowers. Its light rhymes carry the speaker through a landscape of freedom until a clock interrupts the dream. The ending keeps the desire for that nightly return alive, even after waking.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Lavanya Nayak writes poetry in Odia and is associated with Jajpur, Odisha. Her Kabita Live biography describes postgraduate study in Odia and an interest in gardening and reading. Her poem ‘ଅଧା ଅଧା ମୌସୁମୀ’ also appears in Odisha Sambad, where the byline and locality connect the publication to this writer.

In her Kabita Live contribution ‘ପ୍ରଳୟ’, the earth’s devastation prompts a series of urgent questions. The speaker asks why the heavens remain silent while homes disappear and the world loses its capacity to bear violence and arrogance. The poem turns from images of catastrophe towards an appeal for intervention and compassion.

sources.label: Odisha Sambad — ଅଧା ଅଧା ମୌସୁମୀ, 19 July 2022

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Lopamudra Banerjee is a poet, author, editor and translator originally from Kolkata and based in Texas. She has translated Bengali fiction by Ashapurna Devi and Mallika Sengupta into English. In an interview with IPPL Journal, she describes translation as a meeting between another writer’s creation and a new readership, and her collaboration with Priscilla Rice, We Are What We Are, as an exploration of women’s voices, cultural roots and identity.

Her Kabita Live poems make memory and the act of writing inseparable. ‘Absence’ listens for the sounds left by people and moments that have vanished, finding the material of verse in what is missing. ‘True Love Meets Poetry’ brings love into contact with free verse, music and disorder, allowing estrangement as well as intimacy to shape the poem.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Lisa Patnaik, named Lisha Patnaik in her supplied biography, grew up in Damanjodi, Odisha. That account describes an early interest in English poetry and a writing practice continued alongside work in information technology. She presents poetry as a personal space for reflection and solace.

Her two Kabita Live poems return to love through dreams and memory. In ‘I see you!’, a longed-for reunion is revealed as a dream, yet its remembered warmth remains valuable to the speaker. ‘One more love’ follows affection that persists after separation and eventually finds a place in poems themselves. Both works attend to feelings that continue beyond an actual meeting.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: László Aranyi, who also writes as Frater Azmon, is a Hungarian poet whose work moves between poetry, visual imagination and alchemical symbolism. His contributor notes in Word For/Word identify the books (szellem)válaszok, A Nap és Holderők egyensúlya and Kiterített rókabőr. English translations have brought his work to journals including Synchronized Chaos.

In ‘Art’, published here in Gabor Gyukics’s English translation, creation becomes an unsettling experiment. A sewing machine, a dissection table and an alchemist’s cauldron turn the act of making into a struggle with power, imitation and decay. The poem’s repeated image of offspring as caricatures questions what a creator can truly bring to life.

sources.label: Synchronized Chaos — Poetry from Laszlo Aranyi

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Leena Thampi writes English poetry alongside her work as an entrepreneur. Her Literary Vibes contributor note traces her upbringing from Jammu to Delhi and lists collections including Rhythms of a Heart, Autumn Blaze, An Allusion to Time and Embers to Flames. Her writing returns to emotional experience through the seasons, music and the natural world.

Her Kabita Live poems range from the ache of waiting in ‘Gossamer Dreams’ to the sustaining presence of a mother in ‘Golden Womb’. ‘A Kite’s Fate’ asks readers to look beyond appearances and recognise another person’s hidden struggles, while ‘Serendipity’ follows a woman turning hurt into writing. Across these different situations, memory and affection become ways of imagining renewal.

sources.label: Literary Vibes — Leena Thampi poems and contributor note, October 2025

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Lopamudra Mishra’s English poems in Kabita Live explore the ways affection changes a person’s sense of self. In ‘I left behind’, familiar songs, books and dance steps give way to a life reshaped through companionship. The sky and stars remain the same while the speaker describes becoming someone new.

‘I woke up thinking about you’ makes a relationship audible through melody, rhythm and remembered words. A different energy animates ‘I am born different’: woodland, wind and imagined wings accompany a speaker seeking room beyond expectations. Together, these poems move between intimacy and the desire to preserve an individual voice.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Lipika Das’s Odia poems in Kabita Live bring private unease into conversation with the wider world. ‘ଖଵର ପୃଷ୍ଠାରେ ସମୟ’ moves from a storm-damaged garden and rain at a balcony to stories of poverty, discrimination and war. Its images suggest how public suffering can enter the most solitary moments of reading and reflection.

In ‘କୁହେଳି’, questions about light, discovery and identity unfold through the moon, a burning river, butterflies and the sea. Scientific exploration stands beside the difficulty of meeting ordinary human needs. These poems make their argument through shifting images and unanswered questions, inviting the reader to remain with uncertainty.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Lipsa Patel’s Odia contributions to Kabita Live move between inward endurance and the pressures of everyday life. ‘ଚିରସାଥୀ’ asks whether every sorrow can be shared, then imagines pain as a sign of continuing life. Its winding river and difficult arithmetic suggest that living is an ongoing search for a way through.

In ‘ଧୂଆଁ’, smoke becomes an image of damaged trust and a past that continues to trouble the present. ‘କରୋନା ଭଲ ଥିଲା’ uses an ironic refrain to question the expense, pollution and social demands surrounding festivals. The contrast between celebration and a household’s strain gives the poem its sharp, unsettling force.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Manoranjan Sahoo is an Odia poet from Indupur in Kendrapara, Odisha. His collections include Apadebata, Khalihatare and Kichhi Kabita Kichhi Nirabata. Poems translated by Pitambar Naik in Prachya Review bring his observations of hunger, fear and public life to English readers.

His Kabita Live poem ‘ପବନ’ follows something that ordinarily refuses to stay: the wind. Within a flute, breath meets the touch of lips and fingers and discovers another life as music. The short, descending lines slow that movement, allowing an image of freedom to become one of intimacy and renewal.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Meenakshi Goswami is a poet and retired school principal from Sonitpur, Assam. She received a National Award to Teachers in 2022 while leading CNS Higher Secondary School. The Ministry of Education’s citation recognises her work in curriculum development, language learning and children’s wider development. Her poetry collections include The Sensuous Zephyr, Waltzing Words and Lush Echoes.

In ‘Wings Without a Harbour’, her Kabita Live contribution, a wandering speaker leaves sharp words behind for woods, waves and open ground. Singing imperfectly becomes a pleasure rather than a failure, and freedom matters more than reaching a destination. Beneath that delight runs a quieter inquiry into identity and purpose.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Minati Pradhan is a bilingual poet, short-story writer and independent scholar associated with the Vishwaneedam Center for Asian Blossoming. The centre lists her among its executive co-nurturers, and a Madras Institute of Development Studies programme identifies her as a poet and scholar based in Bangalore. Her author profile names the poetry collection A New Dawn and describes an interest in social questions, education and women’s lives.

‘The Power of Time’, her Kabita Live poem, considers time through a series of contradictions. It destroys and heals, brings acceptance yet can awaken grief, and slips beyond the reach of human invention. The final image of remorse remaining in an empty palm gives these abstract questions a tangible, intimate form.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Madhusudan Mishra is a retired Indian Administrative Service officer and the registrar of Jagadguru Kripalu University in Odisha. The university records his earlier service as district collector in Nayagarh, Boudh and Sonepur, as well as a beginning in teaching political science. Alongside this career in administration, his Kabita Live contributions explore memory, affection and the stories attached to place.

‘Sashisena Temple, Sonepur’ retells a local love legend as a celebration of a woman’s freedom to choose. His other poems turn towards the persistence of feeling: letters lost to a river, a schoolmate remembered across decades, and love imagined as light travelling beyond distance. The classroom, riverbank and familiar landscape become places where time passes but emotional memory remains.

sources.label: Jagadguru Kripalu University — Board of Governors biography

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Manas Ranjan Mahapatra is an Odia poet, fiction writer, translator and editor whose literary life remains closely connected with Puri. His work at the National Book Trust included the National Centre for Children’s Literature. In a 2021 interview, he described editing as a commitment to other writers that also sharpened his scrutiny of his own work. His books include the story collection Unit Tinira Premika and the novel Nihsanga.

In ‘ଦିନେ ଫେରିବାବେଳେ ଅନ୍ଧାରରେ’, a friend’s warning about the dangers of walking home in darkness becomes an unexpected argument. The speaker answers that daylight holds wounds of its own, turning a familiar exchange into a terse meditation on human hurt. Its conversational opening and ironic reversal give a small scene a wider moral reach.

sources.label: Odisha Sambad — interview with Manas Ranjan Mahapatra

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Meenakshi Mohan is a Maryland-based poet, educator, painter and children’s writer. Her literary work brings together an interest in visual art, learning and the lives of families. Her books include the poetry collection Symphonies of Life and the children’s books The Gift and The Rainbow in My Room. Matwaala’s author profile also records her editorial work with Inquiry in Education and Confluence.

In Kabita Live’s ‘Waiting’, evening becomes a landscape of prayer: saffron light, trees imagined as monks, and the distant sound of a conch lead towards a small light in a window. The closing images of a mother and a wife give the quiet scene its human centre. The poem allows hope and uncertainty to remain together, without resolving the wait.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Manas Bakshi is a Kolkata-based English-language poet whose writing also extends to the economic history of rural Bengal. His doctorate at the University of Calcutta examined the transition from feudalism to capitalism, and his academic books explore agrarian change and land reform. His poetry collections include In the Age of Living Death, The Midnight Star and Soliloquy of a Sailor.

His Kabita Live poem ‘Tacitly So’ starts with marks on graph paper and follows what those marks cannot fully preserve. Bricks lose a mason’s fingerprints, discarded letters lose the trace of a postman, and felled trees can no longer invite rain. These ordinary remains turn into a meditation on forgotten labour, ecological loss and the way time erases evidence of a life.

sources.label: Creative Flight — Manas Bakshi’s literary and academic profile

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Mahima Gantayat writes poetry and short fiction from Rayagada, Odisha, working in Hindi and English. Her first Hindi poetry collection, An Kahi Baaten, was published by Aditya Bharat in 2026. Speaking at its launch, she described the books in her home and school libraries, along with her family’s literary tradition, as early encouragements to write.

Her English poems in Kabita Live approach memory through familiar places and the ache of absence. In ‘Roots of Childhood’, a tree holds the memory of siblings at play even as adulthood carries them towards responsibilities and new friendships. ‘Echoes of You?’ turns towards the silence left by a once-attentive listener, asking whether the words shared between two people can continue to reach across their distance.

sources.label: Odishabarta — launch of An Kahi Baaten

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Marmasparshee Priyadarshini’s contribution to Kabita Live, ‘The Arrival of Spring’, imagines the season as a correspondence between a woman and the sky. A folded letter becomes a boat of wishes; flowers supply colour and scent to its language. The poem’s movement depends on these small transformations, carrying an intimate gesture into the wider garden.

Punctuation becomes part of that living world: a bird carries a full stop, the breeze turns pages, and the sky sends down pauses with pollen. By the close, butterflies can read a language newly grown among the flowers. Writing and renewal become inseparable in this playful account of how a season answers human longing.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: M. Rudra’s ‘Unshackled Dreams’ brings a voice of protest to Kabita Live. The poem begins with confinement and turns towards the unequal freedom offered to women and men. Its chains and darkening sky make social restriction feel immediate, while the speaker insists on the right to imagine a life beyond it.

An appeal to the Mahabharata stands beside the contemporary image of candles raised in protest. The contrast asks what public gestures can achieve when fear and judgment remain. The closing wish to dream freely gives the poem its direction: towards dignity and possibility, even while the conditions of freedom are still being questioned.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Mrutyunjay Sarangi writes poetry and short fiction in Odia and English and edits Literary Vibes. A retired civil servant and former tribunal judge, he has made literary editing and storytelling a substantial part of his later working life. His English story collections include A Train to Kolkata and Other Stories and The Jasmine Girl at Haji Ali; he also has a body of short fiction in Odia.

His Kabita Live poems put public life under an unsettling light. ‘The Body’ follows a crowd trying to claim an unidentified dead man until a child recognises Gandhi, turning the scene into a question about abandoned ideals. ‘Journey Is On’ builds through repeated contradictions: institutions continue their motions while their human purpose slips away. Both poems use plain speech and narrative momentum to press a moral question.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Manoj Chola’s English poem ‘Crawling Desert’ brings an advancing landscape into the most intimate space: the eyes. Dreams scatter like birds leaving a storm-struck nest, and the ground they leave becomes dry and thorny. The extended image makes a loss of hope feel physical, as though an inner climate has changed.

As the poem moves on, kindness, love and sympathy are described through moisture, heat and snow. Their disappearance widens the desert from private feeling into a fear for human compassion itself. The final arrival of a silent death-chariot leaves this Kabita Live contribution suspended between warning and lament.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Madhu Jaiswal is a bilingual poet and editor from Kolkata. Her poems have appeared in literary journals including Setu, and her editorial work has included anthologies with The Impish Lass Publishing House. In her contributor biography, she describes writing as a way to attend to the inner life, alongside a commitment to compassion and social service.

‘Damsel’, her Kabita Live contribution, tests the distance between a woman’s authority at work and her place at home. The admired professional returns to an unequal burden of household labour, with little room for her own voice. The poem’s plain, insistent account ends with continuing effort rather than resolution, keeping the reader’s attention on the support she is denied.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Mridula Menon’s Kabita Live poem ‘Lost in the Shimmering Glow of Dreams’ follows a change in the way a woman understands aspiration. Youthful delight in imagined possibilities gives way to a more demanding question: what can a dream become without the work that might fulfil it? The poem holds on to hope while asking it to take a practical form.

Its imagery moves from wings and glittering light towards roots and deeds. That movement carries the poem’s central distinction between being enchanted by a future and patiently making one. Written in a direct, reflective voice, it invites the reader to think about how imagination can enrich the life being lived now.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Maid Corbic, also published as Maid Čorbić, is a poet from Tuzla, Bosnia and Herzegovina. His writing has appeared in journals including Synchronized Chaos, and he has taken part in literary communities concerned with peace and human connection. A 2022 interview in Agape Review records his work with the World Literature Forum for Peace and Humanity and the First Virtual Art portal.

In that interview, he describes spirituality, compassion and respect across cultures as important sources of his poetry. For him, writing can connect people and leave something for younger readers to carry forward. His published poem ‘When Love Is Dumb’ approaches those concerns from a more unsettled place, setting loneliness and disappointment beside the hope for a new beginning.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: May Manoj’s ‘Heaven on Earth’ brings its reader into a conversation about the value of an ordinary human life. Short, rhyming stanzas move through laughter, tears and the small acts of care that make a day matter.

The poem’s promise rests in everyday conduct: kindness, humility and forgiveness become ways of making the world more generous. Its direct address gives the verse the warmth of encouragement, asking the reader to recognise a capacity for goodness already close at hand.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Maitreyee B Chowdhury is a Bengaluru-based poet, writer and translator whose work moves between poetry and literary history. Her books include ‘Where Even the Present Is Ancient: Benaras’ and ‘The Hungryalists’, an account of the rebellious poets of Bengal’s Hungry Generation. Her editorial work with The Bangalore Review forms another part of that engagement with literary voices.

In ‘Unfinished’, her contribution to Kabita Live, an intimate address becomes a challenge to poetry itself: what can a poem know of hunger, anger and abandonment? Questions, broken connections and repeated negations resist an easy resolution. The unfinished relationship of the title opens into a larger unease about the distance between words and lived suffering.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Mallika Tripathi writes poetry alongside a career in education. Literary profiles connect her with the Department of Applied Science and Humanities at Feroze Gandhi Institute of Engineering and Technology, Raebareli. Her writing spans Hindi and English, with collections including ‘Oh Son! My Sun!’ and ‘Whispers of the Soul’.

Her Kabita Live poem ‘Angel’ imagines a figure who rises beyond anguish without surrendering to it. Ashes, light and clear sight give the poem its movement from suffering towards endurance. The angel’s distance from worldly attachment is paired with an embrace of others, making compassion and inward strength central to the portrait.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Matralina Pati is a poet, researcher and translator working between Bengali and English. Her literary biographies describe research into marginal Bhasha literatures in English translation at Bankura University. She translated Rudra Pati’s Bengali poems for ‘Monsoon Seems Promising This Year’, bringing another poet’s work into conversation with her own writing.

Her Kabita Live poems question what can be measured and what remains concealed. ‘The Insoluble Sum’ turns calculation into an image of life’s resistance to explanation; the accompanying ‘Deaths and the Accountant’ sharpens that image into a critique of reducing lives to accounts. ‘Bubbles within’ gives loss a fragile, vanishing form, while ‘Matrimony’ contrasts public vows with a truth kept out of sight.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Mahi Rao’s ‘विरह’ (‘Separation’) follows a speaker who longs for a meeting that remains out of reach. Sleeplessness and the brief hope of a glimpse give the poem an intimate scale, while its returning wish to meet keeps longing present from beginning to end.

Lamps, moonlight and the shade of a mahua tree make absence tangible. The beloved is recalled through places and gestures rather than a continuous story. Repetition gives the Hindi poem a song-like movement, holding desire and distance together without resolving either.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Manini Jena teaches Odia at Prananath College in Khordha. Alongside poetry, her journal biography records an interest in criticism of Odia stories and novels. That attention to literature’s making also enters her poems, where the act of writing becomes a subject to question rather than take for granted.

In ‘କବିତା ଲେଖୁଥିବା ଲୋକ’, poetry is discovered in fragrance, a labourer’s sweat and a cuckoo’s call, then threatened by noise and neglect. The poem asks whether writing words is enough to make a poet. ‘ସମୟ ପାଇଁ କିଛି ସମୟ’ turns instead towards withheld speech and the difficulty of apprehending time, giving abstract questions the pressure of breath, skin and the body.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Mitra Samal is a Bhubaneswar-based poet and writer with a background in software consulting. Her work includes poetry, stories and literary interviews, and her collections include ‘Beginning’ and ‘Silence Has a Sound’. Her poems and prose have appeared in journals including Muse India, Madras Courier, Borderless and The Chakkar.

Her Kabita Live poems bring together public freedom and the comforts of everyday life. ‘Remember Freedom’ insists on the right to speak, love and live without fear, using a recurring phrase to keep that possibility alive. ‘Silent Streets’ listens to children, evening prayers and faint bells: its quiet is inhabited, a shared refuge rather than an empty place.

sections.heading: Life and writing.
paragraphs: Malaya Kumar Jati is an English lecturer, poet and literary critic from Odisha. His writing brings together creative verse and an interest in how language is taught and read. He is the author of the poetry collection ‘LIFE: my voice my verse’ and the bilingual grammar book ‘An Easy Way to English’.

In ‘Your Silence Speaks’, published in The Genius, silence becomes a form of intimacy that words cannot quite replace. The poem moves between delight, distance and apprehension, finding both sweetness and unease in what remains unsaid. Its address to a beloved gives these reflections a personal, lyrical shape.
